title: refactor(ir): Extract Expr base class from ScalarExpr for extensibility
body:
Introduce a new Expr base class as the root of all expression types, and rename the previous Expr to ScalarExpr to better reflect its purpose. This refactoring enables future support for non-scalar expressions (e.g., TensorExpr, ArrayExpr) while maintaining type safety and code clarity.

Key Changes:
- Add include/pypto/ir/expr.h with new Expr base class
- Rename Expr → ScalarExpr in include/pypto/ir/scalar_expr.h
- Update all transform tools (ExprFunctor, ExprVisitor, ExprMutator) to work at the Expr base level instead of ScalarExpr
- Update printer, structural_hash, and structural_equal to accept ExprPtr
- Extend field_visitor type traits to support both ExprPtr and ScalarExprPtr
- Update Python bindings to expose both Expr and ScalarExpr classes

Type Hierarchy After Refactoring:
  IRNode
  --Expr (new, generic base)
      --ScalarExpr (renamed, for scalar expressions)
         --Var, ConstInt, Call 
         --BinaryExpr (Add, Sub, Mul, ...)
         --UnaryExpr (Abs, Neg, Not, ...)

title: feat: add CHECK and INTERNAL_CHECK macros for runtime validation
body:
Introduces CHECK and INTERNAL_CHECK macros for streamlined runtime condition validation with appropriate exception types. CHECK throws ValueError for user-facing validation errors, while INTERNAL_CHECK throws InternalError for internal invariant violations.

The implementation uses a template-based CheckLogger class that supports stream-style error message composition and automatically includes source location information in the error output. Both C++ macros and Python functions are provided for consistency across the language boundary.

Additionally, improves backtrace filtering to hide more infrastructure frames including C++ standard library and exception handling code, resulting in cleaner stack traces. The InternalError exception now displays with the module name "pypto" rather than the full qualified name for better readability.

Changes include configuring CMake to use C11 standard with extensions disabled for improved portability, comprehensive test coverage for the new check functions including edge cases with special characters and Unicode, and updated type stubs to expose the new API surface.

title: refactor(ir): add null checks to visitor and mutator base classes
body:
Add INTERNAL_CHECK assertions to validate expression tree invariants in visitor and mutator implementations. This prevents null pointer access and ensures type safety during tree traversal and transformation.

Changes include null checks for binary operation operands (left/right), unary operation operands, and Call arguments. Also added documentation to ExprVisitor class header clarifying the purpose and organization of visitor methods for different node types.

title: Fix backtrace deduplication for Clang debug info
body:
Deduplicate stack frames by PC address to handle Clang's DWARF generation issues where multiple virtual frames are reported for the same program counter with incorrect source locations. Keep only the last frame for each unique PC as it typically represents the actual call site.

Also add "object.h" to the filename filter list to exclude Python object header frames from backtraces.

title: refactor(core): Refactor DataType from enum to class with extensible encoding
body:
Major Changes:
- Convert DataType from enum class to a full-fledged class with static constants
- Encapsulate helper functions as class member methods:
  * GetBit() - get type size in bits
  * ToString() - get string representation
  * IsFloat() - check if floating point type
  * IsSignedInt() / IsUnsignedInt() / IsInt() - check integer types
  * Code() - get underlying type code
- Redesign type code encoding with category-based ranges:
  * Boolean:    0x00-0x0F (16 slots reserved)
  * Signed int: 0x10-0x1F (16 slots reserved)
  * Unsigned:   0x20-0x2F (16 slots reserved)
  * IEEE float: 0x30-0x3F (16 slots reserved)
  * Brain/Hybrid float: 0x40-0x4F (16 slots reserved)
- Eliminate all magic numbers with named constants (k*Code, k*RangeStart/End)
- Update Python bindings from py::enum_ to py::class_ with method bindings
- Update all test code to use new method-based API
- Fix structural_hash.cpp to use Code() method instead of direct cast
- Change BOOL type size from 8 bits to 1 bit

Breaking Changes:
- Python API changed from free functions to instance methods:
  * get_dtype_bit(dtype) -> dtype.GetBit()
  * dtype_to_string(dtype) -> dtype.ToString()
  * is_float(dtype) -> dtype.IsFloat()
  * etc.

title: fix(ir): align EqualVar logic with HashVar for consistent structural comparison
body:

- Replace pointer mapping with ID-based mapping in EqualVar
- Add test case for Var(x)+Var(y) vs Var(a)+Var(a) comparison

title: fix: correct Python type stubs and structural equality implementation
body:
This commit fixes several issues in the IR type system and Python bindings to ensure type correctness and proper structural equality/hashing support.

Key changes include updating the Python type stubs (ir.pyi) to accurately reflect the C++ bindings by adding missing classes (Stmt, UnknownType), fixing type annotations to use covariant Sequence types instead of List, broadening parameter types from ScalarExpr to Expr for binary/unary operations, and moving dtype and shape attributes to the base Type class for better pyright compatibility. The structural_hash and structural_equal functions were updated to accept IRNode instead of just Expr to support Stmt nodes. Additionally, pre-commit configuration and type checking infrastructure were updated to catch these issues earlier.

All changes have been verified to pass pyright type checking and maintain compatibility with existing tests.

title: feat(ir): Add operator registration system with type inference
body:
Implement a comprehensive operator registration system for PyPTO IR that supports automatic type deduction and NumPy-style broadcasting for tensor and tile operations.

Key Features:
- Fluent API for operator registration using REGISTER_OP macro
- Automatic type deduction with compile-time type safety
- Broadcasting support for tensor and tile operations
- Type promotion following standard numeric rules
- Dynamic dimension support (kDynamicDim = -1)

Components Added:
- OpRegistry: Singleton registry for managing operators
- OpRegistryEntry: Type-erased operator configuration with fluent API
- Type inference utilities: BroadcastShapes, PromoteDataTypes, etc.
- TensorType and TileType: N-dimensional and 2D tensor types
- Built-in operators: tensor.{add,sub,mul,div}, tile.{add,sub,mul,div}

Architecture:
- Operators organized by category in src/ir/op/{tensor_ops,tile_ops}/
- Static initialization via REGISTER_OP macro for automatic registration
- Shared type inference utilities in src/ir/op/type_inference.cpp
- Python bindings with complete type stubs

Documentation:
- 02-operator_registration.md: System overview and usage guide
- 03-operator_organization.md: Code organization and design patterns
- src/ir/op/README.md: Developer guide for adding new operators

Testing:
- 18 comprehensive tests covering all operators and edge cases
- Tests for broadcasting, type promotion, and error handling
- All tests passing

This lays the foundation for extensible operator support in PyPTO IR, enabling easy addition of new operations while maintaining type safety and expressiveness.

title: refactor(ir): use map-based Program with GlobalVar for function management
body:
Refactored the Program class to use a map structure (GlobalVar -> Function) instead of a vector, enabling better function lookup and intra-program function calls. This change ensures deterministic ordering of functions (sorted by name) for consistent structural equality and hashing.

Key changes:
- Added GlobalVar class as a special Op type for function references
- Changed Program::functions_ from vector to map with GlobalVarPtrLess comparator
- Added GetFunction() and GetGlobalVar() convenience methods
- Extended reflection system with IsIRNodeMapField trait for map field handling
- Updated transformers (printer, structural_equal, structural_hash) to support map fields
- Updated documentation with GlobalVar usage examples and intra-program call patterns
- Updated Python bindings to expose GlobalVar and new Program interface
- Added comprehensive tests for new functionality

- Add TypeRegistry for mapping IR node types to serialization handlers
- Implement type-specific deserializers for all IR node types
- Expose serialization functionality through Python bindings (serialize/deserialize methods)
- Add comprehensive unit tests for serialization round-trip validation
- Add developer documentation explaining the serialization architecture

The serialization system enables saving and loading IR structures, which is essential for caching, distributed processing, and program persistence.

title: feat(ir): Add infrastructure for synchronization pass (EvalStmt, Sync Ops, PipeType)
body:
This PR introduces the foundational infrastructure required to implement synchronization insertion passes in PyPTO. It enhances the IR with expression statements (`EvalStmt`), defines hardware architecture enumerations (`PipeType`, `CoreType`), and registers synchronization operations.

Changes:
- **IR Core**:
  - Add `EvalStmt` to allow expressions (e.g., function calls) to exist as standalone statements without assignment
  - Update `IRMutator`, `IRVisitor`, `PythonPrinter`, and serialization logic to support `EvalStmt`
  - Expose `EvalStmt` to Python bindings

- **Architecture**:
  - Introduce `include/pypto/ir/pipe.h` defining `PipeType` (MTE1, MTE2, V, etc.) and `CoreType` (VECTOR, CUBE)
  - Expose these enums to Python as `ir.PipeType` and `ir.CoreType`

- **Operators**:
  - Register system synchronization operations (`sync_src`, `sync_dst`, `bar_v`, `bar_m`, `bar_all`) in `src/ir/op/sync_ops/sync.cpp`
  - Extend `Op` and `OpRegistry` to support `PipeType` attribute
  - Annotate existing block operations with their corresponding pipeline types:
    * Memory Ops (`ub_copy_in`, `ub_copy_out`) -> MTE2, MTE3
    * Compute Ops (`mul`, `add`, `sum`, etc.) -> Vector (V)
    * Scalar Ops (`get_block_idx`) -> Scalar (S)

- **Testing**:
  - Add `tests/ut/ir/statements/test_eval_stmt.py` to verify `EvalStmt` creation, printing, and serialization
  - Update `tests/ut/ir/operators/test_block_ops.py` to verify the `pipe` attribute of block operations

title: Add BasicMemoryReusePass
body:
# Implement BasicMemoryReusePass: Memory Reuse Optimization Based on Dependency Graph

## Overview

This PR implements `BasicMemoryReusePass`, a memory reuse optimization pass that analyzes variable lifetimes based on dependency graphs to identify memory sharing opportunities, reducing memory allocation and improving memory efficiency.

## Key Features

- **Lifetime Analysis**: Uses `DependencyAnalyzer` to build dependency graphs and compute variable lifetimes via topological ordering
- **Reuse Identification**: Greedy algorithm identifies variables that can share memory based on:
  - Same memory space (DDR vs UB isolation)
  - Non-overlapping lifetimes (`var1.last_use < var2.def_point`)
  - Sufficient size (`var1.size >= var2.size`)
- **MemRef Sharing**: Implements memory reuse by sharing `MemRef` objects (C++ `shared_ptr`) between variables

## Algorithm

1. Analyze dependency graph using `DependencyAnalyzer`
2. Compute topological order using Kahn's algorithm
3. Calculate lifetime intervals `[def_point, last_use_point]` for each `TileType` variable
4. Identify reuse opportunities using greedy matching within each memory space
5. Apply MemRef sharing via `IRMutator`

## Integration

- Integrated into `OptimizationStrategy.XPlatform` pipeline (after `InitMemRefPass`)
- Exposed via Python bindings for standalone or `PassManager` usage

title: feat(ir): Add unique identifier field to MemRef
body:
## Summary

This PR adds a unique identifier (`id_`) field to the `MemRef` struct to enable better tracking and identification of memory references in the IR. The ID is automatically assigned by `InitMemRefPass` during memory reference initialization.

## Changes

### Core Changes
- **Added `id_` field to `MemRef` struct**: A `uint64_t` field that stores a unique identifier for each MemRef instance
- **Updated `MemRef` constructor**: Now requires explicit `id` parameter (removed default constructor)
- **Updated `InitMemRefPass`**: Automatically generates unique IDs using an internal counter (`next_id_`)

### Serialization Updates
- **Serializer**: Added `id` field to MemRef serialization
- **Deserializer**: Updated to read and validate `id` field from serialized data

### Python Bindings
- **C++ bindings**: Updated `MemRef` class binding to include `id_` field and updated constructor signature
- **Python type stubs**: Updated `ir.pyi` to reflect new constructor signature
- **IRBuilder**: Updated `memref()` helper method to accept `id` parameter

### Testing & Examples
- **Test cases**: Updated all `test_memref.py` test cases to include `id` parameter
- **Examples**: Fixed `sinh_taylor_codegen.py` example to include `id` parameter

## Benefits

1. **Memory Reference Tracking**: Each MemRef now has a unique identifier that can be used for tracking, debugging, and memory reuse analysis
2. **Consistency**: All MemRef instances are now created with explicit IDs, making the code more explicit and less error-prone
3. **Future Extensibility**: The ID field enables future features such as memory reuse optimization passes that need to identify and track specific memory allocations

## Breaking Changes

- `MemRef` constructor now requires 4 parameters instead of 3: `(memory_space, addr, size, id)`
- Default constructor for `MemRef` has been removed
- All existing code creating `MemRef` instances must be updated to include the `id` parameter

## Testing

- All existing tests have been updated and pass
- Pre-commit checks pass (clang-format, cpplint, ruff, pyright)
- Serialization/deserialization tests verify ID persistence

title: [WIP] Codegen refact

## Summary

This PR unifies CCE and PTO code generation under a common base and operator-registry-driven codegen, and includes related IR and documentation updates from the `codegen_refact` branch.

**Highlights:**
- **Codegen refactor**: Introduce `CodegenBase`, remove `ISAMapper`, register per-operator codegen via `f_codegen_cce` / `f_codegen_pto`.
- **IR extensions**: MakeTuple, multi-dimensional TileType, EvalStmt in OpStmts, scalar type validation for control flow.
- **Documentation**: IR verifier docs and CCE codegen doc renumbering.
- **Matmul codegen**: L0C-to-GM storage op and matmul codegen support.

## Changes

### Codegen

- **CodegenBase** (`include/pypto/codegen/codegen_base.h`): Common base for `CCECodegen` and `PTOCodegen` with a unified API for operator codegen callbacks (`GetCurrentResultTarget`, `Emit`, `GetExprAsCode`, `GetTypeString`, `GetConstIntValue`, `GetVarName`).

- **DataType::ToCTypeString**: Extended to cover all DataType variants (e.g. INT8/16, UINT8/16, FP64, etc.). Orchestration codegen uses it instead of a local mapping.
- **PTOCodegen**: Refactored to extend `CodegenBase` and use registry-based `VisitExpr_(Call)`; operator-specific MLIR emission moved into op registration (e.g. block_ops, memory).

- **MakeTuple** and use for shape/offset arguments where appropriate.

- **Scalar type validation** for control flow statements.
- **IR verifier** documentation added/updated; doc renumbering (e.g. 11/13 for verifier and CCE codegen).

### Operators & bindings

- Block ops (elementwise, matmul, memory, unary), sync ops, and tensor ops register CCE and/or PTO codegen where applicable.
- Python bindings and type stubs updated for new/updated APIs and types.

title: feat(tests): Add system test framework with comprehensive documentation
body:
# PyPTO System Tests

This directory contains system-level integration tests for PyPTO. The testing framework (`harness`) is included internally in `tests/st/harness/`. These tests validate the complete compilation and execution pipeline from PyPTO DSL programs to executable code on target platforms.

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Running Tests](#running-tests)
- [Test Configuration Options](#test-configuration-options)
- [Advanced Usage](#advanced-usage)
- [Writing New Tests](#writing-new-tests)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

## Overview

System tests use the internal `harness` package to perform end-to-end validation of PyPTO programs:

1. **PyPTO Frontend**: Defines tensor operations using Python DSL
2. **Compilation Pipeline**: Transforms high-level IR through optimization passes to generate kernels
3. **Simpler Runtime**: Executes generated code on simulator or hardware platforms
4. **Validation**: Compares runtime results against NumPy reference implementations

**Test Flow:**
```
Test Case Definition → Build IR → Generate Kernels → Compile → Execute → Validate
   (Python DSL)       (PyPTO)   (Codegen)        (C++)    (Simpler)  (NumPy)
```

## Prerequisites

### Required Software

- **Python**: Version 3.9 or higher
- **PyPTO**: Installed (`pip install -e .` from project root)
- **Simpler Runtime**: Set `SIMPLER_ROOT` environment variable

### Python Dependencies

- `pytest>=7.0.0` - Test runner (in dev dependencies)
- `pytest-forked` - Required for process isolation between tests
- `numpy` - Reference computations

### Hardware Requirements

- **Simulation Mode** (default): No special hardware required
- **Hardware Mode**: Requires NPU device (e.g., Ascend AI Processor)

## Running Tests

**Important:** The `--forked` flag is required for running system tests.

### Basic Test Execution

Navigate to the PyPTO project root and run tests:

```bash
# Navigate to PyPTO project directory
cd /path/to/pypto-github

# Run all system tests (simulation mode by default)
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked

# Run specific test file
pytest tests/st/runtime/test_matmul.py -v --forked

# Run specific test class
pytest tests/st/runtime/test_matmul.py::TestMatmulOperations -v --forked

# Run specific test method
pytest tests/st/runtime/test_matmul.py::TestMatmulOperations::test_matmul_shapes -v --forked
```

### Platform Selection

Tests can run on simulation or hardware platforms:

```bash
# Run on simulator (default, no hardware required)
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --platform=a2a3sim

# Run on real hardware (requires NPU device)
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --platform=a2a3 --device=0

# Specify different device ID
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --platform=a2a3 --device=1
```

### Verbose Output

Control output verbosity for debugging:

```bash
# Standard verbose mode
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked

# Extra verbose mode (shows test function docstrings)
pytest tests/st/ -vv --forked

# Show print statements and logging
pytest tests/st/ -v -s --forked

# Show full diff for assertion failures
pytest tests/st/ -vv --tb=long --forked
```

### Filtering Tests

Use pytest's built-in filtering capabilities:

```bash
# Run tests matching keyword
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked -k "matmul"

# Run tests NOT matching keyword
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked -k "not matmul"

# Run tests with specific marker
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked -m "slow"

# Skip tests with specific marker
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked -m "not hardware"
```

## Test Configuration Options

The test framework provides extensive configuration through pytest command-line options.

### Available Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `--platform` | `a2a3sim` | Target platform: `a2a3sim` (simulator) or `a2a3` (hardware) |
| `--device` | `0` | Device ID for hardware tests (0, 1, 2, ...) |
| `--strategy` | `Default` | PyPTO optimization strategy: `Default` or `PTOAS` |
| `--save-kernels` | `False` | Save generated kernels and artifacts to disk |
| `--kernels-dir` | `build/tests/st/outputs/output_{timestamp}/` | Custom output directory for saved kernels |
| `--dump-passes` | `False` | Dump intermediate IR after each compiler pass |
| `--codegen-only` | `False` | Only generate code, skip runtime execution |

### Usage Examples

```bash
# Test with PTOAS optimization strategy
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --strategy=PTOAS

# Run hardware tests on device 1
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --platform=a2a3 --device=1

# Save generated kernels for inspection
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --save-kernels

# Save kernels to custom directory
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --save-kernels --kernels-dir ./my_test_outputs

# Enable compiler pass dumps for debugging
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --save-kernels --dump-passes

# Generate code without running (for code inspection)
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --codegen-only --save-kernels

# Combine multiple options
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --platform=a2a3sim --strategy=PTOAS --save-kernels --dump-passes
```

## Advanced Usage

### Saving Generated Code

By default, generated kernels are stored in temporary directories and cleaned up after tests. Use `--save-kernels` to persist them:

```bash
# Save to default location: build/tests/st/outputs/output_{timestamp}/
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --save-kernels

# Save to custom directory
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --save-kernels --kernels-dir ./test_artifacts

# Run single test and save outputs
pytest tests/st/runtime/test_matmul.py::TestMatmulOperations::test_matmul_shapes -v --forked --save-kernels
```

**Output Structure:**

Test directories are prefixed with sequential numbers (e.g., `001_`, `002_`) to avoid name collisions when multiple tests have similar names:

```
build/tests/st/outputs/output_20260205_143022/
├── 001_matmul_64x64/
│   ├── kernels/
│   │   ├── aiv/
│   │   │   └── matmul.cpp          # Generated kernel code
│   │   ├── orchestration/
│   │   │   └── orch.cpp            # Orchestration skeleton
│   │   ├── kernel_config.py        # Simpler runtime configuration
│   │   └── golden.py               # NumPy reference computation
│   ├── pass_dump/                  # (if --dump-passes enabled)
│   │   ├── 001_initial.mlir
│   │   ├── 002_after_pass_x.mlir
│   │   └── ...
│   └── metadata.json               # Test metadata
├── 002_matmul_128x128/
│   └── ...
└── 003_tile_add_64x64/
    └── ...
```

### Debugging with Pass Dumps

Dump intermediate IR representations after each compiler pass to debug transformations:

```bash
# Enable IR pass dumps
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --save-kernels --dump-passes

# The pass_dump/ directory will contain IR snapshots at each optimization stage
# Files are numbered sequentially: 001_initial.mlir, 002_after_pass_x.mlir, etc.
```

This is useful for:
- Understanding how optimization passes transform your program
- Debugging unexpected codegen results
- Learning the PyPTO compilation pipeline
- Reporting compiler bugs with IR snapshots

### Code Generation Only

Generate code without executing on the runtime:

```bash
# Generate kernels without running
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --codegen-only --save-kernels

# Useful for:
# - Validating code generation without hardware/simulator
# - Inspecting generated C++ kernel code
# - Manual orchestration development
# - CI/CD pipelines that only test compilation
```

### Using Optimization Strategies

PyPTO supports different optimization strategies. Select at runtime:

```bash
# Use Default optimization strategy (default)
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --strategy=Default

# Use PTOAS (PTO Accelerator Strategy) optimization
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --strategy=PTOAS

# Combine with other options
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --strategy=PTOAS --save-kernels --dump-passes
```

You can also override the strategy in individual test cases by implementing the `get_strategy()` method:

```python
from pypto.ir.pass_manager import OptimizationStrategy

class MyTest(PTOTestCase):
    def get_strategy(self):
        return OptimizationStrategy.PTOAS
```

### Parameterized Testing

Run tests with multiple configurations:

```bash
# The conftest.py defines standard test shapes
# Tests using the tensor_shape fixture will run with: (64,64), (128,128), (256,256)

# Run all shape variations
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked

# Filter to specific parameter
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked -k "64"
```

## Writing New Tests

### Test Structure

System tests inherit from `PTOTestCase` and implement required methods. See the example below:

```python
"""
Test file: tests/st/runtime/test_my_operation.py
"""
from typing import Any, List
import numpy as np
import pytest
from harness.core.harness import DataType, PTOTestCase, TensorSpec


class TestMyOperation(PTOTestCase):
    def __init__(self, rows: int = 64, cols: int = 64, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.rows = rows
        self.cols = cols

    def get_name(self) -> str:
        """Return a unique test name."""
        return f"my_operation_{self.rows}x{self.cols}"

    def define_tensors(self) -> List[TensorSpec]:
        """Define input and output tensors."""
        return [
            TensorSpec("input_a", [self.rows, self.cols], DataType.FP32, init_value=2.0),
            TensorSpec("input_b", [self.rows, self.cols], DataType.FP32, init_value=3.0),
            TensorSpec("output", [self.rows, self.cols], DataType.FP32, is_output=True),
        ]

    def get_program(self) -> Any:
        """Define the PyPTO program."""
        import pypto.language as pl

        @pl.program
        class MyOperationProgram:
            @pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.InCore)
            def my_operation(
                self,
                a: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32],
                b: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32],
                c: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32],
            ) -> pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32]:
                # Load data to L1 memory
                tile_a = pl.block.load(a, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[64, 64], target_memory=2)
                tile_b = pl.block.load(b, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[64, 64], target_memory=2)

                # Perform operation (example: element-wise add)
                tile_c = pl.block.add(tile_a, tile_b)

                # Store result back to global memory
                out = pl.block.store(tile_c, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[64, 64], output_tensor=c)
                return out

            @pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.Orchestration)
            def orchestrator(
                self,
                a: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32],
                b: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32],
            ) -> pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32]:
                out = self.my_operation(a, b)
                return out

        return MyOperationProgram

    def compute_expected(self, tensors, params=None):
        """Compute expected results using NumPy."""
        tensors["output"][:] = tensors["input_a"] + tensors["input_b"]


class TestMyOperationSuite:
    """Pytest test suite."""

    @pytest.mark.parametrize("rows,cols", [(64, 64), (128, 128)])
    def test_my_operation_shapes(self, test_runner, rows, cols):
        """Test my operation with various shapes."""
        test_case = TestMyOperation(rows=rows, cols=cols)
        result = test_runner.run(test_case)
        assert result.passed, f"Test failed for {rows}x{cols}: {result.error}"
```

### Tensor Initialization Patterns

`TensorSpec` supports flexible initialization:

```python
# Scalar initialization (broadcast to all elements)
TensorSpec("a", [128, 128], DataType.FP32, init_value=1.0)

# NumPy array initialization
TensorSpec("b", [4, 4], DataType.FP32, init_value=np.eye(4))

# Callable initialization (for random data)
TensorSpec("c", [256, 256], DataType.FP32,
           init_value=lambda: np.random.randn(256, 256))

# Zero initialization (default for outputs)
TensorSpec("output", [128, 128], DataType.FP32, is_output=True)
```

### Existing Test Examples

Refer to existing tests for more examples:

- **Matrix Multiplication**: [`tests/st/runtime/test_matmul.py`](runtime/test_matmul.py)
  - Demonstrates matmul operation with L0A/L0B/L0C memory levels
  - Shows parameterized testing with pytest

### Test Fixtures

The [`conftest.py`](conftest.py) provides useful fixtures:

- `test_config`: Session-scoped configuration from CLI options
- `test_runner`: Session-scoped test runner (reused across tests)
- `optimization_strategy`: Current optimization strategy
- `tensor_shape`: Parameterized fixture for standard shapes

### Custom Markers

Use pytest markers to categorize tests:

```python
@pytest.mark.hardware  # Requires --platform=a2a3
def test_hardware_specific(test_runner):
    ...

@pytest.mark.slow  # Long-running test
def test_large_model(test_runner):
    ...
```

### Test Framework Package

The testing framework is located at `tests/st/harness/` with the following structure:

- `core/` - Core test infrastructure (harness, test_runner, environment)
- `adapters/` - Adapters bridging PyPTO to Simpler (program, config, golden generators)

### Test Organization

Tests are organized by execution mode:

- `runtime/` - Tests that execute on hardware or simulator
  - Includes hardware availability detection
  - Automatically skips when hardware unavailable (platform=a2a3)
  - Always runs on simulator (platform=a2a3sim)
- `codegen/` - Tests that only verify code generation
  - Automatically uses --codegen-only mode
  - Does not require Simpler runtime

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

#### Tests Fail or Hang Without --forked

**Problem:** Tests fail with unexpected errors, hang, or produce incorrect results when run without `--forked`.

**Solution:**
```bash
# Always use --forked to run each test in a separate process
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked

# Install pytest-forked if not available
pip install pytest-forked
```

#### ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pypto'

**Problem:** PyPTO is not in the Python path.

**Solution:**
```bash
# Install PyPTO in editable mode
cd /path/to/pypto-github
pip install -e .
```

#### ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'harness'

**Problem:** The internal test package is not in the Python path.

**Solution:** Tests must be run from the project root with pytest:
```bash
cd /path/to/pypto-github
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked
```

The `conftest.py` automatically adds `tests/st/` to the Python path.

#### ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'code_runner'

**Problem:** Simpler runtime is not available.

**Solution:** Set the SIMPLER_ROOT environment variable:
```bash
export SIMPLER_ROOT=/path/to/simpler
```

#### Fixtures Not Found

**Problem:** pytest can't find `test_runner` or other fixtures.

**Solutions:**
```bash
# Run from project root directory
cd /path/to/pypto-github
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked

# Check pytest discovers conftest.py
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --collect-only
```

#### Hardware Tests Skipped

**Problem:** Tests marked with `@pytest.mark.hardware` are automatically skipped.

**Solution:**
```bash
# Run hardware tests on device
pytest tests/st/ -v --forked --platform=a2a3 --device=0
```

### Verification Checklist

Before running tests, verify your setup:

- [ ] PyPTO installed: `python -c "import pypto"`
- [ ] pytest-forked installed: `pip install pytest-forked`
- [ ] In correct directory: `pwd` shows PyPTO project root
- [ ] conftest.py exists: `ls tests/st/conftest.py`
- [ ] harness package exists: `ls tests/st/harness/`
- [ ] Simpler is set up: `echo $SIMPLER_ROOT`

---

For questions or contributions, please refer to the main [PyPTO README](../../README.md).

title: refactor(example): Move orch example to ir_parser
refactor(backend): Split 910B into CCE/PTO backends and refactor ops to use registry
body:
## Summary

This PR splits the monolithic 910B backend into separate **CCE** and **PTO** backends, introduces a **BackendType** enum and **GetBackendInstance()** for passes and codegen, and refactors IR operators (block_ops, sync_ops) and InsertSync pass to obtain pipe/op information from the backend registry instead of hardcoded logic.

**Highlights:**

- **Backend split**: Replace single `Backend910B` with `Backend910B_CCE` and `Backend910B_PTO`, each with dedicated headers (`backend_910b_cce.h` / `backend_910b_pto.h`) and op tables (`backend_910b_cce_ops.cpp` / `backend_910b_pto_ops.cpp`).
- **BackendType & registry**: Add `BackendType::{CCE, PTO}` and `GetBackendInstance(BackendType)` so InsertSync, InferFunctionCoreType, GenerateOrchestration, and `ir.compile` select the backend by type.
- **IR ops refactor**: Block ops (elementwise, matmul, memory, unary, broadcast, reduction, batch_matmul) and sync ops no longer duplicate pipe/codegen logic; they use the backend from the registry (or codegen’s backend) for pipe type and codegen callbacks.
- **Passes & codegen**: InsertSync pass and orchestration/CCE/PTO codegen take `BackendType` (or use the appropriate backend instance). PassManager and `ir.compile()` accept `backend_type` and pass it through.

---

## Changes

### Backend

- **backend.h**: Add `BackendType` enum, `GetBackendInstance(BackendType)`, and extend `Backend` API for op info lookup used by codegen and InsertSync.
- **backend_910b_cce.h / backend_910b_pto.h**: New headers for 910B CCE and PTO backends.
- **backend_910b_cce_ops.cpp / backend_910b_pto_ops.cpp**: New files containing CCE-only and PTO-only op registration (pipe type, codegen funcs).
- **backend_910b.cpp**: Removed; logic split into `backend_910b_cce.cpp` and `backend_910b_pto.cpp`.
- **backend_registry.h/cpp**: Registry extended for "910B_CCE" and "910B_PTO"; used for deserialization and backend creation.
- **soc.h/cpp**: SoC/backend integration updates as needed for the new backend types.

### Codegen

- **CCECodegen / PTOCodegen**: Construct with default backend (CCE or PTO) or from backend pointer; use backend for op lookup in codegen.
- **Orchestration**: `GenerateOrchestration` and `InferFunctionCoreType` take `backend::BackendType` and resolve backend via `GetBackendInstance(backend_type)`.

### IR & passes

- **Op registry**: Simplify op registration; pipe and codegen info come from backend op tables rather than duplicated in IR op code.
- **Block ops** (elementwise, matmul, memory, unary, broadcast, reduction, batch_matmul): Remove local pipe/codegen tables; use backend from codegen or registry.
- **Sync ops**: Align with backend-based pipe/codegen lookup.
- **InsertSync pass**: Accept `backend::BackendType`; use `GetBackendInstance(backend_type)` for pipe lookup when inserting sync ops.

### Python & bindings

- **backend**: Expose `BackendType` enum; keep `Backend910B_CCE` and `Backend910B_PTO` in `__init__.py` and type stubs.
- **compile**: `ir.compile(..., backend_type=BackendType.PTO)` (default PTO); selects codegen and pass backend by type.
- **PassManager**: Default strategy uses `BackendType.CCE` for InsertSync (pipe lookup).
- **passes**: `insert_sync(backend_type)` bound with `BackendType` argument.
- **Type stubs**: `backend.pyi` and `passes.pyi` updated for `BackendType` and `insert_sync(backend_type)`.

### Tests

- **test_backend_910b.py**: Updated for CCE/PTO backend split and registry (e.g. instantiate and test both backend types).
- **test_insert_sync.py**: All InsertSync tests call `passes.insert_sync(BackendType.CCE)`.
- **test_block_ops.py**: Removed or adjusted tests that relied on old op/pipe behavior; block op behavior now backend-driven.

### Build & examples

- **CMakeLists.txt**: Build rules updated for new backend sources (backend_910b_cce_ops, backend_910b_pto_ops, etc.).
- **orchestration_example.py**: Uses `backend_type=BackendType.CCE` (or appropriate type) in `ir.compile()`.

title: refactor(backend): Unify block.l0c_store with block.store and fix CCE pipe types
body:
## Description

### Summary

Refactors the 910B CCE backend to unify `block.l0c_store` with `block.store` pattern and correct pipe type assignments for memory/store operations.

### Changes

#### 1. block.l0c_store Refactor

- **Remove legacy 3-arg format** `(buffer, offset, value)`; only support 6-arg format `(tile, row_offset, col_offset, height, width, output_tensor)`
- **Unify with block.store pattern**: TASSIGN + TSTORE, stride-based offset calculation, Var/TensorType validation, RegisterOutputPointer
- Replaces `TSTORE_L0C` with `TASSIGN` + `TSTORE` for consistency

#### 2. Pipe Type Corrections

| Op | Before | After | Rationale |
|----|--------|-------|-----------|
| `block.store` | MTE2 | MTE3 | UB → DDR (MTE3) |
| `block.l0c_store` | MTE3 | FIX | L0C → UB (FIX pipe) |
| `block.move` | MTE2 | MTE1 | L1 → L0A/L0B (MTE1) |

title: feat(ir): Add ParentStmtAnalysis utility for statement parent tracking
body:
Add a new utility class ParentStmtAnalysis that builds and queries parent-child relationships in IR statement trees. This enables passes to traverse upward in the IR or understand statement context.

Key features:
- Encapsulated design with private members (parent_map_, current_parent_)
- BuildMap() accepts FunctionPtr and traverses function body
- GetParent() queries parent statement (returns nullptr if not found)
- HasParent() checks if statement has a parent
- Clear() enables reusing the same instance

Implementation:
- New header: include/pypto/ir/transforms/utils/parent_stmt_analysis.h
- New source: src/ir/transforms/utils/parent_stmt_analysis.cpp
- Python bindings added to ir.cpp
- Comprehensive tests with 9 test cases including deep nesting validation

Supports all statement types: SeqStmts, OpStmts, IfStmt, ForStmt, etc. Root statements (function body) have no parent as expected.

title: feat(language): Support pl.range() without init_values for simple loops
body: Make RangeIterator generic so pl.range(n) returns just the loop variable (int) instead of a tuple, enabling the simpler `for i in pl.range(n):` pattern alongside the existing iter_args pattern. Add overload signatures for proper type inference.

title: feat(ir): Add passes to flatten nested call expressions
body:
Add three new IR transformation passes and a verification rule to handle nested call expressions and statement structure normalization:

1. FlattenCallExpr - Converts nested calls into three-address code by extracting nested call expressions into temporary variables (_t0, _t1, etc.) Example: c = foo(bar(a)) => _t0 = bar(a); c = foo(_t0)

2. NormalizeStmtStructure - Ensures Function/IfStmt/ForStmt bodies are SeqStmts and consecutive AssignStmt/EvalStmt are wrapped in OpStmts

3. FlattenSingleStmt - Removes unnecessary nesting by replacing single- statement SeqStmts/OpStmts with their content

4. VerifyNoNestedCall - Verification rule to check for nested calls in call arguments, if conditions, for ranges, and binary/unary expressions

Changes include:
- C++ implementation with comprehensive documentation
- Python bindings for all three passes
- Type stubs with complete function signatures
- Extensive test coverage (4 test files with Before/Expected patterns)
- Integration with IRVerifier for automatic verification

title: style(python): Modernize type annotations and add python-style rules
body:
## Summary

Modernize Python type annotations to use built-in generics (Python 3.9+) and establish coding style rules.

title: feat(language): Add unified pl.op.* dispatch API
body:
## Summary

Add a unified `pl.op.*` namespace that auto-dispatches between tensor and block operations based on the first argument's type (`Tensor` vs `Tile`), eliminating the need to explicitly choose `pl.op.tensor.*` or `pl.op.block.*`.

### Key changes

- **`unified_ops.py`** — Dispatch functions for 13 overlapping ops (`add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `maximum`, `exp`, `reshape`, `view`, `matmul`, `row_max`, `row_sum`, `cast`, `reshape`). Binary arithmetic ops auto-select scalar block variants (`adds`/`subs`/`muls`/`divs`) when the Tile rhs is a scalar.
- **`op/__init__.py`** — Exports unified dispatch functions and promotes block-only ops (`load`, `store`, `neg`, `sqrt`, etc.) and tensor-only ops (`create`, `assemble`) to `pl.op.*`.
- **`ast_parser.py`** — Supports 3-segment `pl.op.X` chains alongside existing 4-segment `pl.op.tensor.X` / `pl.op.block.X`. Refactors shared kwarg parsing into `_parse_op_kwargs` (DRY).
- **Tests** — 27 tests using `ir.assert_structural_equal` to verify unified and explicit paths produce identical IR.
- **Docs** — Updated `06-operator_organization.md` and `07-python_syntax.md`.

### Before / After

\`\`\`python
# Before: must choose namespace explicitly
tile_c = pl.op.block.add(tile_a, tile_b)
tile_d = pl.op.block.muls(tile_c, 2.0)
tensor_c = pl.op.tensor.add(tensor_a, tensor_b)

# After: unified dispatch (explicit namespaces still work)
tile_c = pl.op.add(tile_a, tile_b)       # → block.add
tile_d = pl.op.mul(tile_c, 2.0)          # → block.muls (scalar auto-dispatch)
tensor_c = pl.op.add(tensor_a, tensor_b) # → tensor.add
\`\`\`

### Scope

Language module only (\`python/pypto/language/\`). IR-level ops and C++ backend are unchanged.

title: Support Dynamic Shape Parameters in Type Annotations
body:
# Support Dynamic Shape Parameters in Type Annotations

## Background

Currently, PyPTO requires shape dimensions to be compile-time constants (literals) in type annotations. This limitation forces developers to create separate test classes for each shape variation, leading to significant code duplication.

## Current Behavior

When trying to use variables for shape dimensions in type annotations, the parser raises an error:

```python
class TestTileAdd(PTOTestCase):
    def __init__(self, rows: int = 128, cols: int = 128):
        super().__init__()
        self.rows = rows
        self.cols = cols

    def get_program(self) -> Any:
        rows, cols = self.rows, self.cols

        @pl.program
        class TileAddProgram:
            @pl.function
            def tile_add(
                self,
                a: pl.Tensor[[rows, cols], pl.FP32],  # ❌ Error here
                b: pl.Tensor[[rows, cols], pl.FP32],
                c: pl.Tensor[[rows, cols], pl.FP32],
            ) -> pl.Tensor[[rows, cols], pl.FP32]:
                tile_a = pl.op.block.load(a, 0, 0, rows, cols)
                tile_b = pl.op.block.load(b, 0, 0, rows, cols)
                tile_c = pl.op.block.add(tile_a, tile_b)
                out_c = pl.op.block.store(tile_c, 0, 0, rows, cols, c)
                return out_c
```

**Error:**
```
ParserTypeError: Shape dimension must be constant: rows
```

## Impact

This limitation leads to:

1. **Code Duplication**: Testing the same operation with different shapes requires creating nearly identical test classes:
   ```python
   class TestTileAdd64x64(PTOTestCase):
       # Full implementation with 64 hardcoded

   class TestTileAdd128x128(PTOTestCase):
       # Full implementation with 128 hardcoded

   class TestTileAdd256x256(PTOTestCase):
       # Full implementation with 256 hardcoded
   ```

2. **Maintenance Burden**: Any change to the test logic must be replicated across all shape variants.

3. **Limited pytest Integration**: Cannot directly use `@pytest.mark.parametrize` with shape parameters:
   ```python
   # Desired but not working:
   @pytest.mark.parametrize("rows,cols", [(64, 64), (128, 128), (256, 256)])
   def test_tile_add(self, test_runner, rows, cols):
       test_case = TestTileAdd(rows=rows, cols=cols)  # ❌ Fails
       result = test_runner.run(test_case)
       assert result.passed
   ```

## Expected Behavior

Ideally, PyPTO should support one of the following approaches:

### Option 1: Variable Capture in Type Annotations
Allow variables to be captured in type annotations:
```python
rows, cols = 128, 128
a: pl.Tensor[[rows, cols], pl.FP32]  # Should work
```

### Option 2: Dynamic Type Construction
Provide a way to construct types dynamically:
```python
TensorType = pl.Tensor.with_shape([rows, cols], pl.FP32)
def tile_add(self, a: TensorType, b: TensorType, c: TensorType) -> TensorType:
    ...
```

### Option 3: Template-based Approach
Allow parameterized program classes:
```python
@pl.program(shape=[rows, cols])
class TileAddProgram:
    @pl.function
    def tile_add(self, a: pl.Tensor[[pl.SHAPE[0], pl.SHAPE[1]], pl.FP32]):
        ...
```

## Workaround

Currently, the workaround is to use a mapping dictionary:

```python
# Create separate classes for each shape
class TestTileAdd64x64(PTOTestCase):
    # 64 hardcoded
    ...

class TestTileAdd128x128(PTOTestCase):
    # 128 hardcoded
    ...

# Map shapes to classes
TILE_ADD_CLASSES = {
    (64, 64): TestTileAdd64x64,
    (128, 128): TestTileAdd128x128,
}

# Use in pytest
@pytest.mark.parametrize("rows,cols", [(64, 64), (128, 128)])
def test_tile_add(self, test_runner, rows, cols):
    test_class = TILE_ADD_CLASSES[(rows, cols)]
    test_case = test_class()
    result = test_runner.run(test_case)
    assert result.passed
```

This workaround is functional but verbose and doesn't scale well.

## Related Files

- `tests/st/test_case/test_elementwise.py` - Contains examples of the current pattern
- `python/pypto/language/parser/type_resolver.py:297` - Where the error is raised

## Questions for Discussion

1. Is there a technical reason why shape dimensions must be compile-time constants?
2. Would supporting dynamic shapes impact code generation or optimization?
3. Are there other use cases beyond testing that would benefit from dynamic shapes?
4. Which of the proposed solutions (if any) aligns best with PyPTO's design philosophy?

## Environment

- PyPTO version: latest (main branch)
- Python version: 3.10

title: feat: orchestration refactor with tensor ops and dynamic shapes
body:
## Summary

This PR extends orchestration with a new tensor read op, dynamic shapes, tuple returns/unpacking, and fixes function type preservation in the FlattenCallExpr pass.

---

### IR

**`tensor.read`**
- New op: `tensor.read(tensor, indices_tuple)` → scalar value. Implemented in C++ (`DeduceTensorReadType` in `memory.cpp`, registered), Python IR API (`tensor_ops.read`), and orchestration codegen (inline C++ for host-side read with linear index from shape).

**Dynamic shapes**
- `tensor.create` accepts `shape: list[Union[int, Expr]]`; dimensions are normalized via `_normalize_expr`. In orchestration codegen, `CalculateTensorSize` uses `GenerateExprString(dim)` so non-constant dimensions (e.g. variables, expressions) are supported instead of requiring constant tensor shapes.

**Dtype validation**
- Tensor ops that take shape/offset tuples (`tensor.create`, `tensor.view`, `tensor.reshape`, `tensor.assemble`) now require “integer dtype” via `dtype_.IsInt()` instead of only `INT64`/`UINT64`, allowing other integer dtypes where appropriate.

---

### Language

**Tuple return types**
- Return type annotations `tuple[T1, T2, ...]` are resolved in `TypeResolver` (`_resolve_tuple_type`) and yield multiple return types on the function. Parameters still cannot be annotated with tuple types (explicit error).

**Tuple unpacking from calls**
- Assignments like `(a, b, c) = some_call()` are supported for any call that returns a tuple: the RHS is evaluated once, bound to a temporary, and each LHS name is bound to the corresponding `TupleGetItemExpr`. Only simple variable names are allowed as unpacking targets (no nested tuples). Unpacking remains supported for `pl.yield_()` as before.

**`pl.tensor.read`**
- `read` is added to the tensor-only ops set so `pl.tensor.read` is available from the language layer and excluded from generic op dispatch.

---

### Codegen (orchestration)

- **Built-in vs user calls**: `IsBuiltinOp` treats `block.*`, `tensor.*`, and `system.*` as built-in; only non-built-in calls are emitted as task-graph function calls.
- **Tensor ops inline**: Tensor ops are collected separately. `tensor.create` and `tensor.read` get inline C++ (device allocation and host-side scalar read with linear index); `tensor.view` / `tensor.reshape` remain metadata-only (no extra inline code).
- **Dynamic shapes**: Size and index expressions use `GenerateExprString` so non-constant shapes and indices are code-generated correctly.
- **Helpers**: `TryGetVarName` supports both `Var` and `IterArg`; return value and tensor op results use it so orchestration works with iter args.

---

### Bugfix

- **FlattenCallExpr**: When building the new `Function` after the pass, the constructor now receives `normalized->func_type_` so that `FunctionType::Orchestration` (and other function types) are preserved instead of being dropped.

title: fix(pass): Handle OpStmts in InsertSync and MemoryReuse passes
body:
FlattenCallExpr calls NormalizeStmtStructure which wraps consecutive AssignStmt/EvalStmt into OpStmts blocks. Both InsertSyncPass and DependencyAnalyzer (used by MemoryReuse) only handled SeqStmts, silently skipping OpStmts contents. This caused InsertSync to miss cross-pipe dependencies and MemoryReuse to find no TileType variables.

Fix by flattening OpStmts in InsertSync's SeqStmts visitor and adding OpStmts handling to all recursive helpers (ExtractMemRefs, ExtractPipesForMemRefs, HasMemRefAccess, FindFirstAccessIndex), and in DependencyAnalyzer's CollectStmtsInBlock. Also switch PTO codegen test to PTOAS strategy since PTO backend doesn't need sync insertion.

The generated code is missing `set_flag`/`wait_flag` calls that are necessary for correct cross-pipe synchronization. ## Root Cause The `InsertSync` pass does not properly handle `OpStmts` blocks created by the `FlattenCallExpr` pass: 1. **flatten_call_expr** wraps extracted temporary assignments in `OpStmts` blocks (see `flatten_call_expr_pass.cpp:198-206`) 2. **insert_sync** only has handlers for `SeqStmts`, `IfStmts`, and `ForStmt` in its dependency analysis 3. When InsertSync encounters an `OpStmts` block, it treats it as a single opaque statement 4. **Dependencies between statements inside OpStmts are not analyzed** 5. **Result**: No sync instructions are inserted for operations within OpStmts blocks ## Output after InsertSync pass Example **with flatten enabled:** **with flatten disabled:** ### Steps to Reproduce ```markdown Compare generated code with and without `flatten_call_expr`: # In pass_manager.py, comment out FlattenCallExpr: OptimizationStrategy.Default: [ ("ConvertToSSA", lambda: passes.convert_to_ssa()), # ("FlattenCallExpr", lambda: passes.flatten_call_expr()), # Disabled ("RunVerifier", lambda: passes.run_verifier()), ... ] With flatten disabled: sync instructions are present With flatten enabled: sync instructions are missing ``` ### Expected Behavior insert sync op correctly ### Actual Behavior don't have sync op when enable flatten_call_expr pass ### Git Commit ID 3ea32b9ba5f788724ca0d7526a92fb1e4ea9c9f0 ### NPU Kind N/A (not hardware-specific) ### Host Architecture x86_64 ### Additional Context _No response_

body:
## Summary

Add PTO2 (V2) orchestration code generation targeting the `PTO2Runtime*` API, with automatic `PTO2_SCOPE` inference for intermediate tensor lifetime management.

## Changes

### V2 Orchestration Codegen (`orchestration_codegen.cpp`)
- New `GenerateOrchestrationV2()` generating PTO2-format C++ code:
  - `#include "pto_orchestration_api.h"`, `ARG_PTR_`/`ARG_SIZE_` defines
  - `make_tensor_external()` for params/returns, `make_tensor()` for intermediates
  - `PTOParam` arrays with `make_input_param`/`make_output_param`/`make_scalar_param`
  - `pto2_rt_submit_task()` with func_id, worker type, kernel name
  - `float_to_u64()` helper for float scalar params
  - `PTO2OrchestrationConfig` via `aicpu_orchestration_config()`
- `OrchestrationStmtCodegenV2` visitor handling function calls, for-loops, tensor ops, scalar/bool constants, and tuple returns
- `TaskRecord`-based scope analysis: tasks with all-external inputs → outer scope; others → `PTO2_SCOPE(rt) { ... }` inner scope
- V2 config file generation (`kernel_config_v2.py`)

### CCE Codegen Integration (`cce_codegen.cpp`, `cce_codegen.h`)
- `CCECodegen::Generate()` now emits both V1 and V2 orchestration files (`<name>.cpp` + `<name>_v2.cpp`)
- `GenerateConfigFileV2()` for PTO2 kernel config

### Tests (`test_orchestration_codegen.py`)
- `TestOrchestrationV2` class with 4 test cases:
  - `test_v2_basic_structure`: V2 format, includes, ARG defines, external/intermediate tensors, PTO2_SCOPE
  - `test_v2_config_file`: V2 config file generation
  - `test_v2_independent_tasks`: all-external tasks → no PTO2_SCOPE
  - `test_v2_vector_example_dag`: 5-task DAG matching `vector_example` reference (`kernel_add`, `kernel_add_scalar`, `kernel_mul`), scalar params via `float_to_u64`, PTO2_SCOPE wrapping inner tasks

## Scope Inference Algorithm

Tasks are classified based on their input tensor dependencies:
- **Outer scope**: all input tensors are external (function params or return tensors)
- **Inner scope** (`PTO2_SCOPE(rt) { ... }`): any input tensor is an intermediate (produced by another task)

Intermediate tensors produced by outer tasks are declared before the scope; inner-only intermediates are declared inside the scope for proper lifetime management.

title: fix(ir): Treat variables with numeric suffixes as distinct in SSA conversion
body:
## Summary

Fixes issue #170 where the ConvertToSSA pass incorrectly transformed variables with numeric suffixes (like `tmp_0` and `tmp_1`).

## Problem

Variables like `tmp_0` and `tmp_1` were incorrectly treated as versions of the same base variable `"tmp"`, causing the SSA converter to merge them. This resulted in incorrect transformations like `add(tmp_1, tmp_0)` becoming `add(tmp_1, tmp_1)`.

This affected any user code with variables ending in `_<digits>`, which is extremely common in generated code (e.g., flash attention example uses names like `t1_104`, `oiUpdate_87`).

## Solution

The fix simplifies `GetBaseName()` to return names unchanged, treating each variable name as a unique identity. This ensures `tmp_0` and `tmp_1` are converted to `tmp_0_0` and `tmp_1_0` respectively.

**Changes:**
- Simplified `GetBaseName()` in `src/ir/transforms/convert_to_ssa_pass.cpp` to return the name unchanged
- Added regression test `test_variables_with_numeric_suffixes` in `tests/ut/ir/transforms/test_convert_to_ssa_pass.py`

## Testing

- ✅ All 43 ConvertToSSA tests pass (including new regression test)
- ✅ All 1163 unit tests pass
- ✅ Code review completed
- ✅ No regressions detected

## Related Issues

Fixes #170

title: [Bug] `pl.yield_` Loses Type Annotation During Parsing
body:
### Component

Parser

### Description

When using `pl.yield_` with explicit type annotations in PyPTO programs, the type information (shape and dtype) is lost during the parsing phase. The parsed output removes the type annotation entirely, which can lead to type inference issues and reduced code clarity.

### Steps to Reproduce

#### Input Code
```py
@pl.program
class IfElseProgram:
    @pl.function
    def compute_if_else(self, a: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32],
                       b: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32],
                       c: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32]) -> pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32]:
        # ... computation ...
        if i == 0:
            # ...
            out_c = pl.store(result_val, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[64, 128], output_tensor=c)
            out_c_yeild: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32] = pl.yield_(out_c)  # Type annotation present
        else:
            # ...
            out_c = pl.store(result_val, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[64, 128], output_tensor=c)
            out_c_yeild: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32] = pl.yield_(out_c)  # Type annotation present
        return out_c_yeild
```

#### Parsed Output

```py
# 00_frontend.py
@pl.program
class IfElseProgram:
    @pl.function
    def compute_if_else(self, a: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32], b: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32], c: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32]) -> pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32]:
        # ... computation ...
        if i == 0:
            # ...
            out_c: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32] = pl.block.store(result_val, [0, 0], [64, 128], c)
            out_c_yeild = pl.yield_(out_c)  # Type annotation LOST
        else:
            # ...
            out_c: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32] = pl.block.store(result_val, [0, 0], [64, 128], c)
            out_c_yeild = pl.yield_(out_c)  # Type annotation LOST
        return out_c_yeild
```

### Expected Behavior

The type annotation should be preserved during parsing:

```python
out_c_yeild: pl.Tensor[[64, 128], pl.FP32] = pl.yield_(out_c)
```

### Actual Behavior

The type annotation is removed:

```python
out_c_yeild = pl.yield_(out_c)
```

52afb94f8cfdabed586c410602cd53014f6277ae

### NPU Kind

N/A (not hardware-specific)

### Host Architecture

x86_64

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: feat(ir): Add InCore scope support with outlining pass
body:
## Summary

Adds `ScopeStmt` IR node to mark execution contexts (e.g., InCore for AICore sub-graphs) and `OutlineIncoreScopes` pass to extract scopes into separate functions.

## Key Changes

- **ScopeStmt node**: New IR statement with `ScopeKind` enum (currently supports `InCore`)
- **OutlineIncoreScopes pass**: Extracts InCore scopes into `Function(InCore)` definitions
  - Analyzes variable usage to determine inputs/outputs
  - Handles nested scopes recursively with hierarchical naming
  - Generates proper tuple unpacking for multiple outputs
- **DSL support**: `with pl.incore():` syntax in Python
- **Builder API**: `begin_scope`/`end_scope` methods
- **Full cross-layer sync**: C++, Python bindings, and type stubs all updated

## Implementation Details

The pass works by:
1. Analyzing each InCore scope to identify external variable references (inputs)
2. Analyzing subsequent statements to determine which definitions are used (outputs)
3. Extracting the scope body into a new `Function(InCore)` with appropriate parameters and return types
4. Replacing the scope with a call to the outlined function plus output assignments
5. For multiple outputs, creates a temp variable for the tuple result, then unpacks with `TupleGetItem`

## Testing

- ✅ 18 new tests covering:
  - Simple and multiple scopes
  - Multiple inputs/outputs
  - Nested scopes
  - Control flow integration
  - Scope statement construction and parsing
- ✅ All existing tests pass (1283 total)
- ✅ Code review completed
- ✅ Documentation updated and condensed to meet project standards (≤300 lines)

## Example

**Before:**
```python
@pl.function
def main(x: Tensor):
    with pl.incore():
        y = pl.add(x, x)
    return y
```

**After OutlineIncoreScopes:**
```python
@pl.function(type=FunctionType.InCore)
def main_incore_0(x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    y = pl.add(x, x)
    return y

@pl.function
def main(x: Tensor):
    y = main_incore_0(x)
    return y
```

title: [Feature] Support automatic data move insertion pass for flexible incore scope boundaries
body:
### Summary

  ## Background

  PR #186 introduced incore scope functionality, but there's an architectural issue that limits flexibility when adjusting scope boundaries.

  ## Problem
  Currently, users must explicitly write `load`/`store` operations in their frontend code to move data between on-chip and off-chip memory. This creates tight coupling between:
  1. The incore scope boundary definition
  2. The explicit data movement operations in user code

  **Consequence:** If we want to adjust the incore scope boundary, we must manually:
  - Relocate `load`/`store` operations
  - Update which tensors are being loaded/stored
  - Ensure consistency between scope boundaries and data movement

  This makes it difficult to experiment with different scope boundaries and prevents automated scope optimization.


### Motivation / Use Case

  ## Benefits
  1. Flexibility - Easy to adjust scope boundaries without code changes
  2. Automation - Compiler can optimize scope placement automatically
  3. Cleaner frontend - Users focus on computation logic, not data movement
  4. Correctness - Compiler ensures consistent data movement

title: feat(codegen): support inplace function calls in orchestration and extend codegen tests
body:
## Summary

This PR adds support for **inplace function calls** in orchestration codegen and extends/refactors the related unit tests.

## Changes

### 1. Orchestration codegen (`src/codegen/orchestration/orchestration_codegen.cpp`)

- **Inplace semantics**: When a return value is also a function parameter (i.e. the caller passes the same buffer as both input and output), we no longer emit duplicate ARG slots or external tensor declarations for it.
- **Implementation**: From the existing `return_vars`, we exclude variables that are already parameters to obtain `unique_return_vars`. ARG definitions, pointer/size parsing, and `make_tensor_external` are generated only for variables that are return-only.
- **Effect**: Generated C++ for inplace calls is simpler, the argument list matches the actual calling convention, and the same buffer is not declared twice in the ARG list.

### 2. Tests (`tests/ut/codegen/test_orchestration_codegen.py`)

- New test cases for **inplace function calls**, covering the “return value is also parameter” codegen behavior.
- Refactor and extend existing orchestration codegen tests for easier maintenance and regression coverage.

title: [Feature] Tensor type annotations support Scalar variables as shape dimensions
body:
### Summary

## Orchestration DSL type annotation gaps

Two type annotation issues remain in the orchestration DSL that degrade developer experience when writing orchestration functions (e.g. paged attention). Both are non-blocking — the generated IR is correct — but they force users to litter code with `# type: ignore` comments.

### 1. Tensor type annotations do not support Scalar variables as shape dimensions

In orchestration code, tensor shapes are often computed at runtime from config scalars. The type annotation parser (`type_resolver.py:_parse_shape`) only accepts integer literals, so using a Scalar variable in a shape annotation is not supported:

```python
q_tile: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [1])
head_dim: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [2])

# Shape elements are Scalar variables, not int literals — annotation is rejected
oi: pl.Tensor[[q_tile, head_dim], pl.FP32] = pl.create_tensor([q_tile, head_dim], dtype=pl.FP32)
```

Current workarounds:
- Use unparameterized `pl.Tensor` (loses shape/dtype info)
- Add `# type: ignore`

Root cause: `_parse_shape` checks `isinstance(elt, ast.Constant)` and rejects `ast.Name` nodes.

### 2. Passing Python literals as `pl.Scalar` parameters requires `# type: ignore`

The DSL parser correctly converts `int`/`float` literals to `ConstInt`/`ConstFloat` IR nodes at parse time, but static type checkers (pyright/mypy) see a type mismatch between `float` and `pl.Scalar[pl.FP32]`:

```python
# Signature expects pl.Scalar[pl.FP32], but 1.0 is a float literal
pij, mi, li = self.kernel_softmax_prepare(sij, 1.0)  # type: ignore[reportArgumentType]

# Signature expects pl.Scalar[pl.INT64], but 0 is an int literal
mi, li, oi, out = self.kernel_online_update(..., is_first, 0)  # type: ignore[reportArgumentType]
```

Possible solutions:
- Accept `Union[Scalar[T], int, float]` in function parameter type stubs
- Use `@overload` to provide multiple signatures
- Adjust `Scalar.__class_getitem__` to support literal matching

### Context

These issues were identified while building the paged attention orchestration example (`examples/ir_parser/paged_attention_example.py`). The P0 blockers (scalar arithmetic/comparison operators, `pl.min()`/`pl.max()`) have already been resolved.

### Affected files

| File | Relevance |
|------|-----------|
| `python/pypto/language/parser/type_resolver.py` | `_parse_shape` rejects non-literal shape elements |
| `python/pypto/language/typing/scalar.py` | Scalar type definition, no `int`/`float` compatibility |
| `python/pypto/language/parser/ast_parser.py` | Literal-to-IR conversion (works at runtime) |


### Motivation / Use Case

```python
@pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.Orchestration)
def paged_attention(
    self,
    query: pl.Tensor[[2, 16, 128], pl.BF16],
    key_cache: pl.Tensor[[2, 2048, 128, 128], pl.BF16],
    value_cache: pl.Tensor[[2, 2048, 128, 128], pl.BF16],
    host_block_table: pl.Tensor[[2, 2048], pl.INT64],
    context_lens: pl.Tensor[[2], pl.INT64],
    out: pl.Tensor[[2, 2048], pl.FP32],
    config: pl.Tensor[[2], pl.INT64],
) -> pl.Tensor[[2, 16, 128], pl.FP32]:
    """Paged attention orchestration.

    Config layout: [batch, block_num, ...]
    Loops over batch and KV blocks, calling CUBE/VECTOR kernels.
    """
    # Read Scalar parameters from config
    batch: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [0])
    num_heads: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [1])
    head_dim: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [3])
    block_size: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [4])
    block_num: pl.Scalar[pl.UINT64] = pl.tensor.read(config, [5])

    # ✅ Supported: pl.min() Scalar binary op
    q_tile = pl.min(num_heads, 128)
    q_loop = (num_heads + q_tile - 1) / q_tile  # requires +, -, / operators

    for b_idx in pl.range(batch):
        cur_seq = pl.tensor.read(context_lens, [b_idx])
        bn_this_batch = (cur_seq + block_size - 1) / block_size

        for q_idx in pl.range(q_loop):
            # ✅ Supported: Scalar operator overloading
            cur_offset = b_idx * num_heads + q_idx * q_tile  # *, + operators supported

            # ⚠️ Issue 1: Tensor type annotations do not support Scalar variables as dimensions
            oi: pl.Tensor[[q_tile, head_dim], pl.FP32] = pl.create_tensor(
                [q_tile, head_dim], dtype=pl.FP32
            )  # q_tile and head_dim are Scalar variables, not literals
            li: pl.Tensor[[q_tile], pl.FP32] = pl.create_tensor([q_tile], dtype=pl.FP32)
            mi: pl.Tensor[[q_tile], pl.FP32] = pl.create_tensor([q_tile], dtype=pl.FP32)

            # Initialize accumulators
            oi, li, mi = self.kernel_init_inplace(oi, li, mi)

            for bn in pl.range(bn_this_batch):
                # Dynamic views into Q/K/V for current batch and block
                qi: pl.Tensor[[q_tile, head_dim], pl.BF16] = pl.view(
                    query, [q_tile, head_dim], [cur_offset, 0]
                )
                cur_block_idx = pl.tensor.read(host_block_table, [b_idx, bn])

                # ✅ Supported: pl.min() and Scalar operators
                valid_len = pl.min(block_size, cur_seq - bn * block_size)

                kj: pl.Tensor[[valid_len, head_dim], pl.BF16] = pl.view(
                    key_cache, [valid_len, head_dim], [cur_block_idx * block_size, 0]
                )
                vj: pl.Tensor[[valid_len, head_dim], pl.BF16] = pl.view(
                    value_cache, [valid_len, head_dim], [cur_block_idx * block_size, 0]
                )

                # QK matmul (CUBE)
                sij: pl.Tensor[[q_tile, valid_len], pl.FP32] = self.kernel_qk_matmul(qi, kj)

                # ⚠️ Issue 2: literal type-checking issue
                # Softmax prepare (VECTOR)
                pij, mi, li = self.kernel_softmax_prepare(
                    sij, 1.0  # passing literal requires type: ignore
                )  # type: ignore[reportArgumentType]

                # PV matmul (CUBE)
                oi_tmp: pl.Tensor[[q_tile, head_dim], pl.FP32] = self.kernel_pv_matmul(pij, vj)

                # ✅ Supported: Scalar comparison operators
                # Conditional is_first flag
                is_first: pl.Scalar[pl.INT64] = bn == 0  # == operator supported

                # Online update (VECTOR) with inplace accumulators
                out_view: pl.Tensor[[q_tile, head_dim], pl.FP32] = pl.view(
                    out, [q_tile, head_dim], [cur_offset, 0]
                )

                # ⚠️ Issue 2: literal type-checking issue
                mi, li, oi, final = self.kernel_online_update(
                    mi, li, oi_tmp, mi, li, oi, out_view, is_first, 0  # passing 0 requires type: ignore
                )  # type: ignore[reportArgumentType]

    return out
```

title: [Feature] Move minimum Python version from 3.9 to 3.10
body:
### Summary

Raise the minimum supported Python version from 3.9 to 3.10.

### Motivation / Use Case

Python 3.9 reached end-of-life in October 2025. Dropping 3.9 support allows us to:

- Use `match`/`case` (structural pattern matching)
- Use `X | Y` union type syntax in type hints at runtime (PEP 604)
- Use `TypeAlias` (PEP 613)
- Benefit from improved error messages and tracebacks
- Drop compatibility workarounds for 3.9

### Proposed API / Behavior

No API changes. Infrastructure and style updates:

- Update `pyproject.toml` / `setup.cfg` with `python_requires >= 3.10`
- Update CI matrix to drop Python 3.9
- Update documentation and coding style rules referencing "Python 3.9+"
- Audit codebase for opportunities to adopt 3.10+ features

### Alternatives Considered

- Keep 3.9 support: not ideal since it is already EOL and limits use of newer language features.
- Jump to 3.11+: too aggressive; 3.10 is a reasonable next step.

### Additional Context

- [Python 3.9 EOL schedule](https://devguide.python.org/versions/)
- [What's New in Python 3.10](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.10.html)

title: feat(codegen): enhance orchestration codegen with tensor APIs, scalar ops, and paged attention
body:
## Summary

- **Refactor orchestration codegen to use typed tensor APIs**: Replace raw string-based tensor allocation with shape/dtype-aware helpers (`EmitTensorDecl`, `EmitFunctionCall`). Add `GetRuntimeDataTypeString()` for runtime-compatible dtype name mapping (e.g. `DataType::FLOAT32`).
- **Extend `CodegenBase` expression support**: Make `TryGetVarName()` and `GenerateExprString()` virtual for subclass override. Add codegen for `FloorMod`, `Min`, `Max`, comparison ops (`Eq`/`Ne`/`Lt`/`Le`/`Gt`/`Ge`), `ConstFloat`, `ConstBool`, `Neg`, and `Cast`.
- **Add IfOp and ViewOp codegen**: Support `IfStmt` branching and `view` operations in the orchestration layer.
- **Add scalar min/max dispatch**: Introduce `_SCALAR_BINARY_OPS` in `ast_parser.py` so `pl.min(s1, s2)` / `pl.max(s1, s2)` dispatch to `ir.min_()` / `ir.max_()` when arguments are `ScalarType`.
- **Fix tuple param cross-contamination**: Multiple tuple-returning kernel calls (e.g. `kernel_init_inplace`, `kernel_softmax_prepare`) previously shared output params because `GetSSABaseName()` collapsed all `_tuple_tmp_N` names. Now uses per-call unique keys (`_tc_0`, `_tc_1`, ...) with `Call*` pointer coordination to isolate each call's tuple elements.
- **Add paged attention example**: End-to-end orchestration codegen example demonstrating multi-kernel paged attention with FlashDecoding-style online softmax.

title: perf(lint): Speed up clang-tidy with diff-based filtering and batched execution
body:
## Summary
- Add `--diff-base` flag to only lint C/C++ files changed relative to a git ref, reducing file count from ~70 to typically 1-5 on PRs
- Batch files into `jobs` clang-tidy processes instead of spawning one per file, cutting LLVM startup overhead
- Update CI workflow to use `--diff-base=origin/main` for pull requests (pushes to main still lint everything)

### How diff-based filtering works
- Uses `git diff --name-only` to find changed files
- If only source files (`.c`/`.cpp`/`.cc`/`.cxx`) changed, lints only those
- If header files changed, conservatively falls back to full lint (since headers can affect any source)
- If no C/C++ files changed, exits immediately with success

body:
## Summary

- **Pass properties are now tags for verifiers**, not strict prerequisites that block pass execution
- Removes `PassPipeline::Validate()` and the strict requirement check from `PassPipeline::Run()`
- Adds centralized `PassProperties` declarations in `pass_properties.h`
- `VerificationMode` (Before/After/BeforeAndAfter) still runs actual IR verifiers against the program
- Fixes 3 failing `test_cce_codegen` tests that couldn't run `ConvertToSSA` because `TypeChecked` wasn't tracked

## Motivation

Programs created via `@pl.program` are already type-checked, but the pipeline had no way to know this — it only tracked properties produced by earlier passes. This forced users to either add a redundant `TypeCheck` pass or set `initial_properties` manually. With properties as tags, the pipeline runs freely and verifiers catch real issues when `VerificationMode` is enabled.

title: [Feature] Refactor target_memory from int to enum type with generic MemoryScope class
body:
### Summary

Refactor `target_memory` from raw `int` to a proper enum type across C++, Python, bindings, printer, and parser. Introduce a generic `MemoryScope` enum class that can serve as a unified memory scope abstraction.

### Motivation / Use Case

`target_memory` currently uses magic numbers (`1=UB, 2=L1, 3=L0A, 4=L0B, 5=L0C`) throughout the codebase. This causes:

- **Poor readability**: `target_memory=3` is meaningless without checking docs
- **No type safety**: Any int is accepted, invalid values caught only at runtime
- **Fragile validation**: Magic number checks like `if target_memory not in (1, 2)` scattered in code
- **Manual casting**: Backend code does `static_cast<MemorySpace>(memory_val)` from int

A `MemoryScope` enum would be self-documenting, type-safe, and reusable beyond just `target_memory`.

### Proposed API / Behavior

**C++ enum:**
```cpp
enum class MemoryScope : int { DDR = 0, UB = 1, L1 = 2, L0A = 3, L0B = 4, L0C = 5 };
```

**Python (via bindings):**
```python
class MemoryScope(enum.Enum):
    DDR = 0
    UB = 1
    L1 = 2
    L0A = 3
    L0B = 4
    L0C = 5
```

**User-facing API change:**
```python
# Before
tile = pl.block.load(tensor, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[32, 32], target_memory=3)

# After
tile = pl.block.load(tensor, offsets=[0, 0], shapes=[32, 32], target_memory=MemoryScope.L0A)
```

**Printer output change:**
```
# Before: target_memory=1
# After:  target_memory=MemoryScope.UB
```

**Parser:** Should handle both `MemoryScope.UB` (new) and `1` (legacy) formats.

### Affected Files

| Layer | Files |
|-------|-------|
| C++ enum | `include/pypto/ir/memref.h` (new enum or rename `MemorySpace`) |
| C++ op registration | `src/ir/op/block_ops/memory.cpp` (`set_attr<int>` → `set_attr<MemoryScope>`) |
| C++ passes | `src/ir/transforms/init_memref.cpp` (remove manual int→enum casts) |
| C++ backend | `src/backend/910B_CCE/backend_910b_cce_ops.cpp` |
| Python bindings | `python/bindings/` (expose `MemoryScope` enum) |
| Python IR ops | `python/pypto/ir/op/block_ops.py` (`target_memory: int` → `MemoryScope`) |
| Python DSL | `python/pypto/language/op/block_ops.py` |
| Type stubs | `python/pypto/pypto_core/` |
| Printer | Kwargs printing (output enum name instead of int) |
| Parser | Kwargs parsing (accept enum name, support legacy int) |
| Tests | `test_init_memref.py`, `test_cce_codegen.py`, `test_matmul.py`, printer tests |

### Alternatives Considered

- **Keep int, add constants**: e.g. `UB = 1, L1 = 2` — less type-safe, no IDE autocomplete on the type itself
- **Reuse existing `MemorySpace`**: The existing enum in `memref.h` has the same values but is tied to memref semantics. A separate `MemoryScope` could be more generic and usable across different contexts

### Additional Context

The existing `MemorySpace` enum in `include/pypto/ir/memref.h` already defines the same values (`DDR, UB, L1, L0A, L0B, L0C`). Consider whether `MemoryScope` should replace, extend, or alias `MemorySpace`.

Currently affected operators: `block.create_tile`, `block.load`, `block.move`.

title: [Bug] Program printer drops FunctionType when printing functions inside @pl.program
body:
### Component

Printer

### Description

When a function is decorated with `@pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.InCore)` and wrapped in a `@pl.program`, the Python printer loses the `type` parameter. The standalone function printer (`VisitFunction`) correctly handles it, but the program printer (`VisitProgram`) hardcodes `@pl.function` without checking the function type.

**Root cause:** In `src/ir/transforms/python_printer.cpp`:
- `VisitFunction()` (line 887-893) correctly checks `func->func_type_` and prints the type parameter
- `VisitProgram()` (line 1068) hardcodes `stream_ << "@" << prefix_ << ".function\n"` without checking the function type

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a function with a non-default FunctionType:

```python
import pypto.language as pl

@pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.InCore)
def test_simple_alloc(input_a: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32], output: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32]) -> pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32]:
    tile_a: pl.Tile[[64, 64], pl.FP32] = pl.block.load(input_a, [0, 0], [64, 64], target_memory=1)
    tile_b: pl.Tile[[64, 64], pl.FP32] = pl.block.add(tile_a, tile_a)
    result: pl.Tensor[[64, 64], pl.FP32] = pl.block.store(tile_b, [0, 0], [64, 64], output)
    return result
```

2. Observe that printing the standalone function correctly shows `@pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.InCore)`
3. Create a program from the function and print it — the type parameter is missing

### Expected Behavior

The program printer should output the function type when it's not `Opaque`:

```python
@pl.program
class test_simple_alloc:
    @pl.function(type=pl.FunctionType.InCore)
    def test_simple_alloc(self, ...) -> ...:
        ...
```

### Actual Behavior

The program printer drops the function type:

```python
@pl.program
class test_simple_alloc:
    @pl.function
    def test_simple_alloc(self, ...) -> ...:
        ...
```

### Git Commit ID

fb9a1e0dff7feb642a5d183ee4d7f99baf2cb359

### NPU Kind

N/A (not hardware-specific)

### Host Architecture

aarch64

### Additional Context

**Suggested fix** — In `VisitProgram()`, line 1068, replace:
```cpp
stream_ << GetIndent() << "@" << prefix_ << ".function\n";
```
with:
```cpp
stream_ << GetIndent() << "@" << prefix_ << ".function";
if (func->func_type_ != FunctionType::Opaque) {
    stream_ << "(type=" << prefix_ << ".FunctionType." << FunctionTypeToString(func->func_type_) << ")";
}
stream_ << "\n";
```

This matches the logic already used in `VisitFunction()` (lines 889-892).
