title: refactor(lint): route operator-name literals through the registry getter
body:
## Summary

`.claude/rules/operator-identity-checks.md` requires an operator-name literal to reach a comparison through `get_op(...)`, which raises on an unregistered name, rather than as a bare string. A bare `call.op.name == "tile.reshaep"` silently evaluates to `False`; routed through the getter the same typo raises `ValueError` at the comparison site. 369 bare literals across 34 files still did the unrouted comparison, so renaming an operator today can silently drop coverage or take a wrong branch instead of failing.

This converts all of them and adds a pre-commit gate so the count cannot grow back. All 145 distinct names resolve against the live registry, so no operator needed registering and no site needed the rule's documented fallback. There is no behavior change for compiled programs: every converted expression evaluates to the same operator name it did before. The observable difference is at import and comparison time — a stale name now raises instead of quietly comparing unequal.

Two of the converted sites were actively silent rather than merely fragile:

- **`python/pypto/debug/torch_codegen.py`** — `_CROSS_CORE_SPLIT_OPS` was four bare literals behind `if op_name in _CROSS_CORE_SPLIT_OPS`. Renaming `tile.tpop_from_aiv` would drop that op's handler and send the call down the fallback codegen path with nothing failing.
- **`tests/ut/ir/transforms/test_flatten_tile_nd_to_2d.py`** — twelve `assert "tile.batch_matmul" not in names` assertions pass *vacuously* once the operator is renamed, surviving as green coverage of nothing.

## Changes

- **`tests/lint/check_op_name_literals.py`** (new) — AST-based gate, wired into `.pre-commit-config.yaml` beside `check-no-broad-raises`. It parses rather than greps, so prose in comments and docstrings is never flagged. It reports four shapes: direct `==`/`!=`, `in`/`not in` against a collection literal, a sequence compare against a `.op.name` comprehension, and a module-level operator-name collection.
- **32 test files** — 364 literals routed through the getter. A name used once in a file is inlined as `ir.get_op("x").name`; a name used twice or more gets a module-level `_OP_*` constant, so the literal is validated once at import instead of being re-resolved at every comparison.
- **`python/pypto/debug/torch_codegen.py`**, **`python/pypto/language/parser/ast_parser.py`** — 5 literals in product code, including the silent membership branch above.

Literals by shape: 244 direct `==`/`!=`, 6 collection membership, 55 module-level collection elements, 64 sequence-compare / bound-list membership / `.count(...)` arguments.

The gate was hardened during review; three reported defects were each reproduced before being fixed, and each ships with a regression case. `frozenset(...)` / `set(...)` / `list(...)` / `tuple(...)` builders are unwrapped before the literal scan, so the immutable form this checker's own remediation message recommends is covered. Bound-collection tracking is per lexical scope with shadowing on reassignment, so a `names` holding operator names in one function cannot cause a false positive in another. Exemptions match the exact `ast.Constant` node, so a construction literal cannot suppress a real comparison of the same name on the same line.

**Scope the gate deliberately excludes.** Callee names carry no dot and are never reported, keeping `"k1"`, `"consumer"` and `"main_incore_1"` out of scope as the rule requires. Construction and name-keyed lookups (`ir.Op(...)`, `get_op(...)`, `create_op_call(...)`) are exempt, as are `@pytest.mark.parametrize` lists feeding `get_op(op_name)` — the getter already raises on a typo there. Two blind spots are documented in the checker's module docstring: dispatch tables whose *keys* are operator-name literals (e.g. `_OP_MAP` in `torch_codegen.py`), and a literal passed into a helper that performs the comparison internally. The known instances of the latter are converted here; neither is detectable without widening the heuristic or adding interprocedural analysis, so both are left for a separate decision.

No IR, API, or migration impact, and no follow-up is required by this range.

## Verification

All commands ran in the transaction's validation runner at the pushed head `cb4f3001`, which refuses to run unless `HEAD` matches the prepared commit and the checkout is clean before and after:

- `python -m pytest tests/ut -n auto --maxprocesses 8 -q`: exit 0 — 9187 passed, 2 skipped in 144.04s (both skips pre-existing)
- `ruff check tests python`: exit 0
- `ruff format --check tests python`: exit 0
- `python tests/lint/check_op_name_literals.py`: exit 0
- `python tests/lint/check_no_broad_raises.py`: exit 0
- `python tests/lint/check_headers.py`: exit 0 — 1037 files
- `python tests/lint/check_english_only.py`: exit 0

Run separately against the same tree:

- `python tests/lint/check_docs_en_zh_parity.py`, `check_docs_nav.py`, `check_docs_symbol_coverage.py`: exit 0
- Gate self-test — 20 cases: all four shapes flagged, the three review-reported defects each reproduced-then-fixed, and nine false-positive guards silent (callee names, already-routed literals, already-routed `frozenset`, the registry's own `get_op(x).name == x` tests, construction calls, `@pytest.mark.parametrize` lists feeding `get_op`, non-operator dotted strings, mixed-type collections, single-element collections)

title: fix(test): pin the C++ log level around every unit test
body:
## Summary

The C++ logger's threshold is process-global and `LOG_WARN` / `LOG_INFO` are gated on it, so a test that lowers it and never restores it mutes the diagnostics every later test in the same process asserts on. Those assertions then fail against an empty stderr for a reason that has nothing to do with the code under test — the outcome depends only on test order.

`tests/ut/core/test_logging.py` sets the threshold in ~15 tests and restores none of them, so whichever ran last decides what the rest of the session can observe. Running its `NONE` case before `TestCapacityGatedReuse::test_fallback_repacks_legacy_on_genuine_overflow` hides MemoryReuse's "fell back to the legacy packing" warning and fails that test against `''`:

```text
pytest "tests/ut/core/test_logging.py::TestSetLogLevel::test_set_log_level_none" \
       "tests/ut/ir/transforms/test_memory_reuse.py::TestCapacityGatedReuse::test_fallback_repacks_legacy_on_genuine_overflow"
# AssertionError: assert 'fell back to the legacy packing' in ''
```

It passes on `main` today only by luck: the file's last-executed test happens to set `INFO`. Any `-k` filter, xdist split, or test appended to that file flips it. The same shape previously reached the unit suite from `tests/st/conftest.py`, which set the global level in `pytest_configure` with an `ERROR` default; #2274 has since scoped that to a per-item thread-local override.

After this change a unit test's stderr assertions no longer depend on what ran before it.

## Changes

- `tests/ut/conftest.py`: new autouse `_reset_log_level` fixture pinning the level around every unit test, mirroring the existing `_reset_backend_singleton`. It snapshots the session baseline at conftest import — before any test can mutate it, so `PYPTO_LOG_LEVEL` is still honoured — restores it before and after each test, and clears any main-thread override. Tests that choose their own level are unaffected: the reset runs first, so their own set still wins. Also adds an `initial_log_level` fixture exposing that baseline.
- `include/pypto/core/logging.h`, `python/bindings/modules/logging.cpp`, `python/pypto/pypto_core/logging.pyi`, `python/pypto/pypto_core/__init__.pyi`, `python/pypto/__init__.py`: restoring the level requires reading it back, and `set_log_level` had no counterpart. Adds `LoggerManager::GetGlobalLevel`, exposed as `pypto.get_log_level` across the binding, stubs, and package exports. It reports the **process-global** threshold rather than `GetLevel()`'s thread-aware value, so a save-restore pair cannot promote a temporary thread override into the global.
- `tests/ut/core/test_logging.py`: contains the module's own mutations, and adds `TestLogLevelIsolation` (the invariant that a sibling's level must not survive into a later test, plus a warning-reaches-stderr canary) and two tests pinning the getter contract, including that it ignores a thread override.
- `docs/en/dev/03-logging.md`, `docs/zh/dev/03-logging.md`: document `get_log_level` and the save-restore pair, and correct the ST section, which still described `--pypto-log-level` as a `pytest_configure`-time `set_log_level` call.

**Interface change:** one addition, `pypto.get_log_level()`. Nothing is removed or renamed, and no compiler behaviour changes — the only non-test source change is a new read-only accessor. No migration step and no follow-up are implied.

**Known limitation, deliberately not changed here:** an explicit `PYPTO_LOG_LEVEL=error pytest tests/ut` still fails `test_fallback_repacks_legacy_on_genuine_overflow`, because the fixture honours the operator's chosen baseline rather than overriding it and that test asserts on stderr. This is pre-existing and is not a leak; the new canary test skips in that mode. Making that test pin the level it needs would be a separate change.

## Verification

All commands ran at the pushed head `cea7a102`, through the push transaction's validation runner unless noted:

- `cmake --build build --parallel`: exit 0
- `python -m pytest tests/ut -n auto --maxprocesses 8 -q`: exit 0 — 9191 passed, 2 skipped in 144.57s
- Regression that fails on `main` and passes here: `pytest "tests/ut/core/test_logging.py::TestSetLogLevel::test_set_log_level_none" "tests/ut/ir/transforms/test_memory_reuse.py::TestCapacityGatedReuse::test_fallback_repacks_legacy_on_genuine_overflow"`: exit 0 — 2 passed
- `python -m ruff check .`: exit 0 — all checks passed
- `python -m ruff format --check .`: exit 0 — 961 files already formatted
- `python -m pyright`: exit 0 — 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations

Recorded before the transaction, at the same tree:

- Original report, both suites in one process: `pytest tests/st/codegen "tests/ut/ir/transforms/test_memory_reuse.py::TestCapacityGatedReuse" tests/ut/core/test_logging.py tests/ut/pass/test_diagnostic_instrument.py`: exit 0 — 123 passed, 30 deselected
- The new isolation tests were confirmed to have teeth: with the fixture temporarily set to `autouse=False`, both fail; restored, both pass
- `clang-format --dry-run --Werror` on the two touched C++ files: exit 0
- `npx markdownlint-cli2 --config tests/lint/.markdownlint.yaml` on the two touched docs: 0 issues

title: ci: move ci.yml's self-hosted jobs onto the toolchain bundle
body:
Moves every self-hosted job in `ci.yml` off the per-machine conda environments and onto a pinned toolchain bundle: `clang-tidy`, `codegen-tests` (cpu runners) and `system-tests`, `system-tests-direct`, `dist-system-tests`, `pypto-lib-model` (npu runners). `daily_ci.yml`'s `qwen3-perf` follows too, since its host setup mirrors `dist-system-tests`. conda itself is untouched on every runner.

## Why

Two machines in the fleet were measured before this:

| | dev box | CI runner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python 3.10 | openEuler rpm mixed into an HCE2 system | absent — only 3.9 |
| `g++-15` | self-built 15.2.1, `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` | conda 15.2.0, `aarch64-conda-linux-gnu` |
| ccache | 3.7.12 | 4.10 |
| package repos | openEuler 23.03 | HCE2 |

Nothing in CI noticed. Both built and tested green while compiling with different compilers, and 3.7.12 silently ignores `CCACHE_NAMESPACE` — the mechanism that stops a `pto-isa` bump from reusing objects built against the old ISA (#1139).

The bundle is one versioned tarball carrying CPython, GCC + libstdc++, uv and ccache, identified by one sha256, built and verified in [pypto-tools/pypto-toolchain](https://github.com/pypto-tools/pypto-toolchain). It depends on the host only for a kernel, glibc >= 2.28, binutils and glibc-devel.

## What changes here

`setup-ci-job` gains a `toolchain` input (`conda` | `bundle`, default `conda`), and the six jobs above that use the action pass `bundle`. `clang-tidy` does not go through the action — it enters the bundle directly in `ci.yml`. Every job is switched, and reverted, on its own.

Three deliberate behaviour changes on the bundle path:

- **The venv drops `--system-site-packages`.** Nothing outside it is depended on now. This also retires the trap that flag created: a failed install in the venv is masked by a copy of `pypto` in the base env, and four conda envs on one runner carry one today. torch is now installed into the venv, costing ~30-60s per job from a warm pip cache.
- **torch is pinned to 2.10.0**, the version the conda fleet already carries. Isolating the venv removed the only thing that was pinning it — with `--system-site-packages`, pip saw conda's copy and skipped the install, so 2.10.0 held by accident rather than by decision. Unpinned, pip resolved to 2.13.0 and `tests/st/codegen/torch/test_torch_codegen_paged_attention.py` began failing its golden compare deterministically at max abs diff 7.35e-02 against a 5e-2 tolerance. Both sides of that comparison run as plain torch over bf16 inputs, so a torch upgrade moves it with no PyPTO change involved. Which change inside torch shifts the result is not established here; the pin keeps this PR a toolchain migration and nothing else, and a torch bump can arrive in a commit that says so.
- **The bundle is sourced after CANN's `set_env.sh`, not before.** `set_env.sh` prepends its own directories to `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`; conda got its precedence by prepending `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` last. ptoas needs `GLIBCXX_3.4.29` and the host libstdc++ stops at 3.4.28, so the bundle's copy has to stay first.

`activate.sh` keeps its contract exactly — one `source activate.sh`, `BASH_SOURCE`-relative so a task-submit child with a truncated env snapshot still finds it — so none of the ~60 call sites change. The generated file is self-tested before anything depends on it: it is assembled by this step and so is the one thing `verify` cannot speak for, and the test asserts what the build will really run (python 3.10, `g++-15` major >= 15, and a ccache that honours `namespace` at all — probed rather than version-matched, since 3.x drops `CCACHE_NAMESPACE` with no error).

## Entering the bundle

Both the check and the activation go through `pypto-toolchain` itself:

```yaml
- run: |
    pypto-toolchain verify --require python=3.10 --require 'gcc>=15' --require 'ccache>=4.8'
    bundle_env="$(pypto-toolchain export)" || exit 1
    eval "$bundle_env"
```

`export` re-emits the selected bundle's own `activate.sh`, resolved through the same install root and `current` symlink that `verify` resolves. The two cannot name different bundles, which naming a path from this side could not guarantee.

**No new key in any runner's `.env`.** An earlier revision of this PR added a `TOOLCHAIN_BUNDLE_ROOT` override for a differently-laid-out host; it is gone, because it reintroduced exactly that split and promised a portability the bundle does not have. `/opt/pypto/toolchain/<version>` is compiled into the bundle's gcc and python — `cc1plus` carries the string and `sysconfig` reports it to every extension build — so a bundle unpacked elsewhere is subtly broken. Relocation is a symlink at `/opt/pypto`, or the install root in the host's own `pypto-env.conf`; `pypto-toolchain` resolves both, and this action follows it there by asking rather than by naming a path.

`verify` asserts capabilities rather than a bundle version, so the fleet can be upgraded without a commit here. `ccache >= 4.8` is a correctness requirement, not hygiene: below it `CCACHE_NAMESPACE` is silently ignored, and that is what scopes the compile cache to the pinned pto-isa commit (#1139).

## Verification

The full `ci.yml` pipeline went green on the bundle at `711be09d`: `clang-tidy`, `codegen-tests`, `system-tests`, `system-tests-direct`, `dist-system-tests`, `pypto-lib-model`, plus `unit-tests`, `system-tests-a5sim`, `pre-commit` and `toolchain`. The current head changes how those jobs enter the bundle, so that pipeline is re-running now.

`daily_ci.yml` is still uncovered and I cannot dispatch it myself: this branch lives on a fork, this account has only triage on `hw-native-sys/pypto`, and `qwen3-perf` wants the org's `[self-hosted, linux, arm64, npu]` runner, which a fork run cannot reach. It needs a `workflow_dispatch` from someone with write here — happy to hand off the exact ref.

The bundle was installed from zero on a runner that had no system python3.10 and no gcc-15 outside conda; `pypto-toolchain verify` passes there. Bundles are additionally verified on AlmaLinux 9 — newer than the build image, so `libffi.so.8` and OpenSSL 3 exercise the SONAME mismatch — on every release.

Rollback is deleting the six `toolchain: bundle` lines and restoring `clang-tidy`'s two steps to conda. conda is untouched on every runner.

title: docs(rules): sort KNOWN_ISSUES entries and rescope AI file length limits
body:
## Summary

The known-issues tracking rule told an assistant to append each new entry to the
end of `KNOWN_ISSUES.md`. Once that file carries a trailing section for entries
nobody has touched in months, "append" silently files fresh entries into that
section — unsorted, and labelled stale. This defines the file's layout and
ordering so placement is mechanical rather than positional, and separately
recalibrates the `.claude/` length limits so each one measures the cost it is
actually protecting against.

No source, build, or test behavior changes; these files govern assistant
workflows only.

## Changes

- `.claude/rules/problem-handling.md`: specifies the two-section layout (active,
  then stale) on top of the existing entry format, and defines sorting within
  each section — severity high to low, then date newest first, where an entry's
  date is the most recent one it records. Adding, updating, or removing an entry
  is now an insert or move to the sorted position; migration across the
  two-month line is spelled out. The worktree write recipe anchors on the
  neighbouring heading and requires a unique match instead of appending, since
  the end of the file is no longer a valid insertion point.
- `.claude/rules/documentation-length.md`: replaces the single 200-line cap on
  everything under `.claude/` with limits scoped by load cost. Rules load into
  every session, so their binding constraint is the directory total: they keep
  the 200-line per-file cap and gain a 2500-line aggregate budget, with the
  check command and the instruction to merge or delete rather than split (a
  split leaves the aggregate unchanged). Skills load only when invoked, so only
  `SKILL.md` is capped at 200 lines while its reference files fall under the
  500-line documentation limit — which is what the progressive-disclosure layout
  already assumed.
- `.claude/rules/error-checking.md`, `.claude/rules/plans-and-proposals.md`:
  condensed from 208 and 201 lines back under the cap, with no guidance dropped
  — the error-message examples move inline, and the test-strategy example loses
  its sub-bullets while still naming all three test files.
- `.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md`: its documentation checklist asserted
  the old single "AI rules/skills ≤200 lines" limit, which the change above
  makes wrong for skill reference files and incomplete for rules. It now checks
  each class, including the aggregate budget.

## Verification

- The insertion recipe was exercised against the real file for both anchor
  forms (a named entry heading, and the `# Stale` heading for an entry sorting
  last among active entries), and for a duplicated anchor, which aborts without
  writing under both `python3` and `python3 -O`.
- `pre-commit run --files <the changed paths>`: exit 0. `check-headers`,
  `check-english-only`, `check-docs-en-zh-parity`, `check-docs-nav`,
  `check-docs-symbol-coverage`, `check-no-broad-raises`, large-file, end-of-file,
  trailing-whitespace and `markdownlint-cli2` all passed; C++ and Python hooks
  skipped with no matching files. No hook modified a file. This ran twice: once
  against the working tree and once inside the push transaction against the
  pushed commit.
- No unit-test run: the change touches no code path under `python/`, `src/`, or
  `include/`.

title: docs(examples): restore the in-DSL if/else dynamic valid_shape pattern
body:
## Summary

`examples/intermediate/06_dyn_valid_shape.py` and both of its system tests told
users that selecting a tile's valid length with an in-DSL `if`/`else` fails
`ConvertToSSA` with *"used outside its defining scope"*, and steered them to
hoist the choice to the caller. That limitation is gone — the JIT specializer's
`_BodyTransformer.visit_If` drops then-branch-introduced names before visiting
the else-branch, so the else-branch binding is a fresh local instead of a
cross-branch alias. The example now shows the natural pattern again, and the
`@pl.jit` path it depends on is covered by tests down to generated PTO.

No product code changes; this is examples, docs and tests only. Nothing a caller
depends on changes, and there is no migration step. The example's public names do
change: it now exports `dyn_valid_shape_if_else` and `dyn_valid_shape_loop`
alongside the existing `dyn_valid_shape`, and the two system tests were updated
to match.

The old note also missed a distinction worth documenting: under `@pl.jit` a
scalar **parameter** is a specialization constant, inlined at every use site. An
`if`/`else` over scalar parameters is therefore resolved at specialization time
and folds to a constant `valid_col`, one kernel per scalar tuple. Selecting a
branch at runtime requires reading the values from a tensor, which is what the
restored kernels do.

## Changes

- `examples/intermediate/06_dyn_valid_shape.py`: dropped the stale "JIT note"
  and its caller-side workaround, which also pointed at comments in
  `examples/models/qwen3_jit/` that do not exist. Restored two kernels beside
  the scalar-parameter one: `dyn_valid_shape_if_else` reads
  `[is_last, last_valid_len, full_len]` from a config tensor and picks `vlen`
  with `if`/`else`; `dyn_valid_shape_loop` loops with a runtime trip count and
  takes the partial length on the last block. Both lower to a real `scf.if`
  feeding the tile's `valid_col`. Documented the specialization-constant rule.
- `examples/intermediate/__init__.py`: package docstring line for `06` matches
  the restored contents.
- `tests/st/codegen/dsl/`: each test now exercises the kernel it is named for.
  The two files had drifted into near-duplicates that both called the
  scalar-parameter kernel, so neither covered the `if`/`else` or the loop. They
  stay lowering-only smoke tests.
- `tests/ut/codegen/test_dynamic_valid_shape_if_else.py`: six tests covering the
  `@pl.jit` path down to PTO — `scf.if` survives specialization, `valid_col` is a
  runtime operand rather than a folded `%c<n>` literal, `pad=3` is preserved, and
  `scf.for` plus `scf.if` both appear for the loop. A negative control pins the
  specialization-constant semantics by asserting the scalar-parameter form does
  fold to `%c48`.

Reverting `visit_If` fails all five runtime-branch tests, so the previously
missing coverage is what allowed the documentation to drift.

## Verification

- `cmake --build build --parallel`: exit 0
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/`: exit 0 — 9,219 passed, 2 skipped
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/codegen tests/ut/jit tests/lint -q`: exit 0 — 1,172 passed
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/codegen/test_dynamic_valid_shape_if_else.py -q`: exit 0 — 14 passed
- `python -m pytest tests/st/codegen/dsl -q`: exit 0 — 11 passed
- `ruff check examples/intermediate tests/ut/codegen tests/st/codegen/dsl`: exit 0 — all checks passed
- `ruff format --check examples/intermediate tests/ut/codegen tests/st/codegen/dsl`: exit 0 — 51 files already formatted
- `python examples/intermediate/06_dyn_valid_shape.py`: exit 0 — all four specializations lower

The system tests are lowering-only and run no device, so this change carries no
on-device numerical evidence.

title: docs(ir): fix stale MemRef and TileView examples
body:
## Summary

Every Python example under `docs/{en,zh}/dev/ir/` that builds a `MemRef` or a `TileView` was written against an API that has since changed, so none of them ran. Copying one out of the docs is the normal way to learn these types, and doing so produced an `AttributeError` or a `TypeError` instead of IR. Nothing executes documentation snippets in CI, which is why the drift went unnoticed. After this change every snippet runs against a local build, and the `MemRef` reference table describes fields the class actually has.

Three independent breakages, all documentation-only — no source, test, or interface change, and no migration step:

- **`TileView` is immutable.** Its fields are read-only and every value passes through the constructor, so the documented build-then-mutate form raised `AttributeError: property of 'TileView' object has no setter`.
- **`MemRef` changed shape.** It names an allocation (`base_`) and a byte range within it (`byte_offset_`, `size_`). It has no `addr_` or `id_` field, and no overload takes a bare `ConstInt` first, so `ir.MemRef(ir.ConstInt(...), size, id)` raised `TypeError: __init__(): incompatible function arguments`.
- **The serialization example never ran at all**, even before the API drift: it serialized an undefined `tile_var`, used an undefined `shape` and `span`, and asserted `len(valid_shape) == 2` on a `valid_shape` equal to the full shape — which the `TileType` constructor clears, making it 0.

## Changes

- `docs/{en,zh}/dev/ir/02-types.md`: four `MemRef` call sites and two build-then-mutate `TileView` blocks rewritten. `MemRef` examples use the base-name form `ir.MemRef("mem_left_0", 0, 512)`, which maps one-to-one onto the fields the class has; `TileView` examples pass every field to the constructor. Each `valid_shape` is now a real sub-region, because one equal to the full shape is cleared and would vanish from the very example introducing it. Prose describing `MemRef` as carrying "address, size, and id" corrected, and pointed at the field table.
- `docs/{en,zh}/dev/ir/01-hierarchy.md`: the `MemRef` field table listed `addr_`, `size_`, and `id_` — two of which do not exist. Replaced with `base_`, `byte_offset_`, `size_`, `is_pinned_`, `slot_count_`, and `slot_index_`, plus a line on `MemRef` being a `Var` subclass and on the `same_allocation` / `may_alias` predicates. The `TileView` table gained the five fields it omitted: `blayout`, `slayout`, `fractal` (a size in **bytes**, not elements), `pad`, and `compact`.
- `docs/{en,zh}/dev/ir/04-serialization.md`: the example now defines `span`, builds a real `tile_var` from the `TileType`, and asserts on a genuine `[8, 16]` sub-region of a `[16, 16]` tile, so the round-trip assertion is meaningful rather than vacuous.

The DSL-annotation form `pl.MemRef(addr, size, id)` in `02-types.md` is deliberately unchanged: that is the parser's annotation surface and it is correct.

The Chinese mirrors carry byte-identical code blocks; only tables and prose are translated.

## What a reviewer should check

- The `MemRef` field table in `01-hierarchy.md` against `include/pypto/ir/memref.h:42-126`, and the `TileView` table against `include/pypto/ir/type.h:303-311`.
- That preferring `ir.MemRef("mem_left_0", 0, 512)` over the still-supported legacy `ir.MemRef(addr, size, id)` is the right call for IR-internals docs. The legacy form works, but it synthesizes a base name from `id` and reinforces the `addr_`/`id_` model this PR removes from the table.
- The deliberate use of a partial `valid_shape` in each example, which follows from `ClearRedundantFullValidShape` (`src/ir/type.cpp:53-57`).

## Verification

- `cmake --build build --parallel`: exit 0
- Every rewritten snippet executed against that build: 7/7 pass, including the serialize/deserialize round-trip. The pre-fix forms were confirmed to fail exactly as described (`AttributeError`, `TypeError`, and `len == 0`), so the examples exercise the current API rather than passing vacuously.
- `mkdocs build --strict`: exit 0, with no link warning for any changed file. This caught a defect mid-change: the Chinese cross-reference anchor was written `#内存引用-memref`, but python-markdown's ASCII slugify strips CJK, so the anchor that resolves is `#memref`.
- `pre-commit run --from-ref upstream/main --to-ref HEAD`: exit 0 — check-headers, check-english-only, check-docs-en-zh-parity, check-docs-nav, check-docs-symbol-coverage, check-no-broad-raises, check-op-name-literals, check-added-large-files, end-of-file-fixer, trailing-whitespace, markdownlint-cli2

## Follow-up not in this PR

Nothing executes doc snippets, which is why four broken blocks and a dead assert went unnoticed. A lint over opt-in-tagged Python blocks would close the class, but it needs a build in the pre-commit environment — which is exactly why `check_docs_symbol_coverage.py` parses `__all__` with `ast` instead of importing. Worth a separate discussion.

Separately, `mkdocs build` reports ~30 pre-existing broken CJK anchors across `docs/zh/` from the same ASCII-slugify behaviour. They are untouched here.

title: feat(ir): reject Acc->GM stores with unsupported dst dtype
body:
## Summary

The cube fix-pipe narrows an accumulator on its way to global memory, but only into a fixed destination set — `INT32/FP32/FP16/BF16` on Ascend910B, `INT32/FP32/FP16` on Ascend950. PyPTO applied no such check, so a split-K matmul assembled into an int8/int16 tensor compiled all the way through codegen and was rejected by ptoas at `pto.tstore` verification, against a line in a generated `.pto` the user never wrote. A single bad dtype choice also tripped a second, unrelated-looking op — an int8 zero-init lowers to a `pto.texpands` with the same illegal dtype — so the late diagnostic named two symptoms and never the cause. This adds an `AccToGmStoreValid` IR property verified right after `InferTileMemorySpace`, so the failure now arrives during passes with the source span of the offending statement, as one error rather than two.

The placement is load-bearing. Legality is a property of the tile's **memory space**, not of the user-visible dtypes: the identical DSL program is legal when its matmul result routes through Vec (an explicit `pl.cast` narrows in the vector unit) and illegal when it stays in Acc. The check therefore cannot move earlier — for example to the DSL — without wrongly rejecting the Vec form.

## Changes

- `include/pypto/backend/common/backend_handler.h`, `.../910B/`, `.../950/`: new `SupportsAccToGmDtype(DataType)` predicate holding the per-arch whitelist beside the existing `SupportsBf16AtomicAdd`. Adding a backend means supplying its set; no pass branches on `BackendType`.
- `src/ir/verifier/verify_acc_to_gm_store.cpp`: the verifier. Walks `tile.store`, and flags one whose source tile is Acc-resident and whose GM destination dtype is outside the backend's set. The message names the arch, the legal set, and both workarounds. It no-ops when the backend is unconfigured or the tile's memory space is unresolved — guessing a profile there would reject programs the real target accepts.
- `include/pypto/ir/transforms/ir_property.h`, `pass_properties.h`, `src/ir/transforms/ir_property.cpp`, `src/ir/verifier/property_verifier_registry.cpp`: register `AccToGmStoreValid`, produce it from `InferTileMemorySpace`, and add it to `GetVerifiedProperties()` so the pipeline auto-verifies it.
- `python/bindings/modules/passes.cpp`, `python/pypto/pypto_core/passes.pyi`: expose the new enum value, keeping the three layers in sync.
- `docs/{en,zh}/dev/passes/99-verifier.md`: document the rule, its placement rationale, and the fix.
- `tests/ut/jit/test_split_k.py`: three rejection cases (int8 atomic, int16 atomic, int8 non-atomic — the whitelist is independent of the `atomic` kwarg) plus `test_int8_dest_via_vec_still_compiles`, which guards against an over-strict check by asserting the Vec-routed form still compiles.

### Behavior change beyond int8/int16

The verifier is keyed on the backend whitelist, so on **Ascend950 it also rejects bf16 Acc→GM, including non-atomic stores**, which previously compiled. That is correct per pto-isa's kirinX90 `CheckAcc2gm` (no bf16 there) and closes a real gap: ptoas accepts that store under `--pto-arch a5`, so it previously failed later against the pto-isa `static_assert`. The existing `SupportsBf16AtomicAdd` codegen guard is retained rather than folded in — it also covers Vec-sourced bf16 atomic stores, which this verifier does not see.

No migration step. A program this now rejects could not have produced a working kernel.

## Verification

- `pre-commit run --files <15 changed paths>`: exit 0, all hooks passed (includes `check-headers`, `check-docs-en-zh-parity`, `check-op-name-literals`, `clang-format`, `cpplint`, `markdownlint-cli2`, `ruff`, `pyright`)
- `cmake --build build --parallel`: exit 0
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/jit/test_split_k.py -q`: exit 0, 14 passed
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/ tests/lint/ -n auto --maxprocesses 8 -q`: exit 0, 9253 passed, 2 skipped

The last three ran through the push transaction's validation runner, pinned to the pushed commit.

title: test(st): right-size fp32 matmul golden tolerances
body:
## Summary

`test_matmul_mixed_add_btranspose[16-64-128-a2a3]` intermittently failed golden
validation on the real NPU with a single-element FP32 mismatch
(`Mismatched elements: 1/2048`, abs diff 1.26e-5 at a golden of -0.0488).

The 910B cube accumulates a matmul's K reduction in a different order than
torch's single-pass BLAS reference, so an FP32 golden comparison drifts by a few
ULP of the **partial sums** rather than of the result. Measured across 489 device
runs of these cases at K=64..128: median 1.1e-5, peak 3.4e-5 absolute. That
drift is set by the partial-sum magnitude and does not shrink with the result
magnitude, so on a cancellation-heavy element — where `torch.isclose`'s
`atol + rtol * |golden|` bound collapses to roughly `atol` — it exceeds the
threshold while every other element passes.

The five plain FP32 matmul cases now validate at `rtol=atol=1e-4`. Against that
`1e-4` floor the peak measured drift is 0.34x, leaving ~3x margin even on an
element whose golden is ~0 and where `rtol` contributes nothing. No product code
changes and no behavior change for users; this only widens test tolerances to the
drift the hardware legitimately produces.

## Changes

- `tests/st/runtime/ops/test_matmul.py`: add one shared
  `_FP32_MATMUL_RTOL`/`_FP32_MATMUL_ATOL` pair (1e-4) documenting the mechanism,
  and apply it in `TestMatmul`, `TestMatmulBTranspose`, `TestMatmulATranspose`,
  `TestMatmulABTranspose`, and `TestMixedAddBTrans`. Each override is guarded by
  `if config is None`, so a caller that passes an explicit `RunConfig` — the
  AutoL0, shared-KV, and a-transpose cases all do — keeps its own tolerance.

Two points that reviewers may want to weigh in on:

- **This is not a K-split case.** #1945 right-sized a set of FP32 matmul s-tests
  and justified it as "the device reduces the two K-halves in a different order".
  That mechanism is absent here: `choose_l0_tile(16, 64, 128)` at FP32 returns
  tile `(m=16, n=128, k=64)`, i.e. K-iters = 1, and the generated cube kernel is
  a single `TMATMUL` over the full K=64 in native `float`. The reduction-order
  drift comes from the cube's internal accumulation within one instruction, so
  the shared comment here describes that instead of reusing the K-split wording.
- **Scope is wider than the one test that flaked.** Because no K-split is
  required to produce ~1e-5 of drift, the non-transposed and transposed sibling
  cases are exposed too. Over 300 device runs they peaked at 0.835x of the old
  1e-5 threshold — closer to failing than the 0.654x peak of the case that
  actually flaked — so fixing only `TestMixedAddBTrans` would have left the more
  exposed cases behind.

## Verification

Run by the push transaction against the pushed commit `55e22f8`:

- `cmake --build build --parallel`: exit 0
- `ruff check .`: exit 0, all checks passed
- `ruff format --check .`: exit 0, already formatted
- `pyright`: exit 0, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/ -n auto --maxprocesses 8`: exit 0, 9255 passed, 2 skipped
- `python -m pytest tests/st/runtime/ops/test_matmul.py --platform a2a3 --device 0`:
  exit 0, 58 passed, 171 deselected (real 910B)

Additional evidence gathered while diagnosing, on the real 910B. "Ratio" below is
the worst per-element `|diff| / (atol + rtol * |golden|)`, so >1 means the run
fails:

- 189 runs of the previously flaking case with fresh random data each: 0 failures
  at 1e-5; peak absolute drift 2.29e-5; worst ratio 0.654 at 1e-5, 0.065 at 1e-4.
- 300 runs of the four sibling cases: 0 failures at 1e-5; peak absolute drift
  3.43e-5; worst ratio 0.835 at 1e-5, 0.084 at 1e-4.
- The drift at the smallest-magnitude golden element is ~4.8% of the array's peak
  drift, so a failure needs a large drift to land on a near-zero element — which
  is why the observed CI rate was low rather than deterministic.

title: feat(codegen): emit MLIR source locations in generated .pto
body:
## Summary

PTO codegen emitted no MLIR `loc()`, so when the ptoas verifier rejected an operation the only location it could report was a line in the generated `.pto` — a file the user never wrote, and never sees at all under `@pl.jit`. ptoas propagates MLIR locations verbatim into its diagnostics, so emitting the `Span` that every IR node already carries gives every ptoas error class source attribution without duplicating any of the backend's constraint knowledge into PyPTO. After this change a rejected op reports the user's `.py` line and column instead. Locations are on by default and can be turned off, in which case the emitted `.pto` is byte-identical to before.

The accuracy of the attribution rests on which span is used. The location is bound at two levels: the enclosing statement in `PTOCodegen::VisitStmt` is primary, and a `Call`'s own span refines it only when it is nested inside that statement's span. The containment test is what makes this correct — `ConvertTensorToTileOps` rebuilds the tile ops it synthesizes carrying the enclosing *function*'s span while preserving the `AssignStmt` span, so across two of this repository's own kernels (`test_pto_codegen_paged_attn.py`, `test_pto_codegen_ops.py`) only 17–35% of post-pass `Call` spans are still statement-nested. Reading `Call::span_` alone would report the `def` line for most operations.

## Changes

- `src/codegen/pto/pto_codegen.cpp`, `include/pypto/codegen/pto/pto_codegen.h`: add a `SpanScope` RAII guard and `LocSuffix()`; `Emit()` now appends `loc("file":line:col)`. Adds the statement-level and containment-checked Call-level binding described above. Unknown spans and spans without a filename emit nothing, leaving those operations exactly as before.
- `src/codegen/pto/pto_control_flow_codegen.cpp`: route the 18 region-brace, separator and block-label lines through a new `EmitStructural()`. MLIR's trailing location is legal only at the end of a complete operation, so annotating `scf.for … {`, `} else {`, `}` or `^bb0(…):` would make the module unparseable. `scf.yield`, `scf.condition`, `pto.tmov` and `pto.set_validshape` remain real operations and keep their locations.
- Prologue operations are covered as well: `pto.make_tensor_view` from the parameter span, `pto.alloc_multi_tile` from the base variable, and hoisted `pto.alloc_tile` from the function. `arith.constant` stays unannotated because the constants section is deduplicated across every use, so no single span fits it.
- `python/bindings/modules/codegen.cpp`, `python/pypto/pypto_core/codegen.pyi`, `python/pypto/backend/pto_backend.py`, `python/pypto/ir/compile.py`: thread the new `emit_source_loc` flag across the C++, binding and stub layers, add `compile(..., emit_source_loc=...)`, and read the `PYPTO_EMIT_PTO_LOC` environment default. ptoas ships independently of PyPTO, so this switch exists to recover from a ptoas build whose parser rejects a trailing location without requiring a PyPTO rebuild.
- `tests/ut/codegen/test_pto_codegen_source_loc.py`: new coverage for per-operation locations, the statement-not-`def`-line attribution, structural lines carrying no location, unannotated constants, source-path escaping, the byte-identical disabled output, and the environment matrix.
- `tests/ut/_pto_loc_common.py` and four existing test files: assertions that anchor on the end of an operation (`endswith`, `strip() ==`) and helpers that slice a type from the end of a line now drop the trailing location first.

## Behavior and interface notes

- Default output changes: generated `.pto` operations now carry a trailing location. Generated `.pto` grows by roughly 40% on the paged-attention kernels (about 112 bytes per operation, dominated by the absolute source path). Set `PYPTO_EMIT_PTO_LOC=0` or pass `emit_source_loc=False` to restore the previous output exactly.
- `PTOCodegen::Generate` and `codegen.PTOCodegen.generate` gain a third parameter, defaulted, so existing callers are unaffected.
- **ptoas acceptance is confirmed by CI.** This was developed without a `ptoas` binary available, so it could not be checked locally. It has since been covered on this PR: `system-tests`, `system-tests-direct`, `dist-system-tests`, `system-tests-a5sim` and `pypto-lib-model` all run with a real `PTOAS_ROOT` at the pinned ptoas (`PTOAS_VERSION=v0.54` in `toolchain/versions.env`) and all pass with locations enabled, on a2a3 device and the A5 simulator. Real kernels therefore assemble and run with the trailing `loc(...)` in place.
- Follow-up, not included: propagating the original op's span in `ConvertTensorToTileOps` instead of the shared function span would improve column accuracy here and every other span consumer. The containment rule above makes this change correct without it.

## Verification

- `cmake --build build --parallel`: exit 0, clean build.
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/ -n auto --maxprocesses 8 -q`: exit 0, 9273 passed, 2 skipped.
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/core/test_error.py -n auto --maxprocesses 8 -q`: exit 0, 41 passed.
- `ruff check .`: exit 0, all checks passed.
- `ruff format --check .`: exit 0, 964 files already formatted.
- `pyright`: exit 0, 0 errors, 0 warnings.
- `pre-commit run --all-files`: exit 0, all 17 hooks passed.
- `ctest --test-dir build`: exit 0, 1/1 passed.
- `python tests/lint/clang_tidy.py --diff-base upstream/main`: exit 0, all checks completed.
- Full CI on this PR head: every required check passed, including the five ptoas-backed system-test suites listed above.

All of the above ran in the working checkout at exactly the pushed commit, through the publication workflow's validation runner.

title: fix(ir): track buffer roots through control flow

## Summary

Track buffer provenance through loop and conditional control flow without asserting false aliases. Loop returns now preserve all possible init/yield roots when execution is not guaranteed, and IfStmt results merge branch provenance conservatively.

title: [RFC] Compiler-driven whole-function AutoTile and graph-partitioning AutoFuse
body:
## Summary

Introduce compiler-driven tiling and fusion for explicitly selected tensor-level PyPTO functions:

- `auto_tile=True` treats the complete function as one fixed subgraph. It must produce one feasible,
  exactly replayable kernel plan or reject the function with an actionable diagnostic. It never
  partitions the graph or silently falls back per operation.
- `auto_fuse=True` may partition the function's tensor DAG into feasible convex groups, then plan
  and emit each group under the same kernel-model contract.

Both features are experimental and opt-in. The compiler never applies whole-function AutoTile or
AutoFuse implicitly: the programmer must place the corresponding explicit function attribute.
Unmarked functions follow the existing compilation pipeline unchanged.

The first upstream milestone is the Ascend 910B vector-only whole-function AutoTile path. It keeps
the user's tensor DAG intact and automatically selects the spatial grid, physical tile/strip shape,
streaming or materialization strategy, pipeline depth, buffer lifetimes, and emitted one-kernel
algorithm.

This project is inspired by the graph partitioning, tiling, retention, and ordering ideas in the
[VNRC submission](https://github.com/huawei-csl/mlsys-2026-graph-scheduling-vnrc-submission), which
placed second in the systems track of the
[MLSys 2026 Graph Scheduling Competition](https://github.com/yarongmu-google/MLSys#track-a-systems-engineering--winners).
The compiler integration is intentionally narrower and more conservative: a selected schedule is
an executable algorithm contract, not merely a low numerical score.

## Motivation

PyPTO lets experts describe high-performance tiled kernels directly, but a user who already has a
small tensor DAG must currently make many coupled low-level decisions by hand:

- where and how to tile the output;
- whether reductions should materialize or stream;
- which values remain live in UB/L1/L0 and when storage can be reused;
- which loops are genuinely eligible for software-pipeline overlap;
- how many SPMD work units to launch;
- and which device-specific algorithm is both legal and profitable.

Those choices are difficult to make independently. For example, a larger tile can reduce GM traffic
but exceed on-chip capacity; a lower modeled roofline is invalid unless emission actually constructs
the assumed double-buffered loop; and a fused intermediate saves GM traffic while extending its
on-chip lifetime.

The project therefore treats planning and emission as one contract:

> A selected plan specifies the kernel algorithm. Every priced lifetime, transfer, overlap, split,
> and retained value must be reproduced by emitted PyPTO IR.

This gives users a higher-level option without weakening the explicit DSL. Hand-written schedules
remain supported and are the reference point for correctness and performance comparisons.

## Proposed API and behavior

### Whole-function AutoTile

```python
class RmsNormProgram:
    @pl.function(attrs={"auto_tile": True})
    def rms_norm(
        self,
        x: pl.Tensor[[512, 512], pl.FP32],
        gamma: pl.Tensor[[1, 512], pl.FP32],
    ) -> pl.Tensor[[512, 512], pl.FP32]:
        square = x * x
        mean = pl.row_sum(square) * (1.0 / 512.0)
        inv = pl.rsqrt(mean + 1e-5)
        return x * inv * gamma
```

The compiler captures the complete tensor DAG and either:

1. validates it against a backend-specific capability surface;
2. selects one feasible schedule;
3. rewrites the whole function into one planned SPMD kernel algorithm; and
4. consumes the marker;

or rejects it before downstream code generation. A rejection must not leave a partial kernel,
report, or PTOAS invocation.

`auto_tile` is distinct from `AutoTileMatmulL0`: the former plans a complete tensor function, while
the latter remains the downstream local L0 tiler for already formed matmul tile operations.

### Compiler feedback

The annotation should not turn scheduling into a black box. At `INFO` level the compiler prints one
concise selected-plan line. A normal compilation also writes a versioned JSON descriptor and a
tile-centric pseudocode report. For the `[512,512]` RMSNorm above, the current M1 implementation
reports:

```text
AutoTile[kernel]: vector schedule=materialized grid=24x1 work_units=24
  tile=22x512 stages=1/1/1 peak_ub=147552 full_peak_ub=147552
  reduction_model=grounded pointwise_model=grounded modeled_cycles=17580.3
```

The corresponding text report explains one representative work unit rather than drawing all 24
copies:

```text
AutoTile schedule for kernel
backend: Ascend910B vector (AIV)
schedule: materialized
grid: 24x1 = 24 work units
representative logical region: [22x512]
UB peak: 147552 bytes streamed, 147552 bytes full-region

spmd 24 work units:
  region = balanced_partition(block_idx)
  body: materialize logical=[22x512]
    x = GM.load(logical=[22x512], physical=[24x512])
    gamma = GM.load(logical=[1x512], physical=[1x512])
    square = tensor.mul(x, x)
    total = tensor.row_sum(square)
    lifetime ends: square
    mean_square = tensor.muls(total, 1 / 512)
    inverse_rms = tensor.rsqrt(mean_square + epsilon)
    normalized = tensor.row_expand_mul(x, inverse_rms)
    lifetime ends: x, inverse_rms
    y = tensor.col_expand_mul(normalized, gamma)
    lifetime ends: normalized, gamma
    GM.store(y)
```

This tells the programmer that the compiler chose 24 row partitions, keeps the full hidden axis in
each work unit, DMA-pads the 22 logical rows to 24 physical rows, materializes the complete RMSNorm
DAG on chip, and releases each value after its last use. Streaming schedules similarly show serial
initialization/tails, rolled pipeline loops, persistent statistics, and ping/pong slots. The JSON
contains the same facts for tooling; its schema is versioned but not initially promised as a stable
public API.

The Ascend 910B target descriptor used by this decision contains all 48 AIV cores. The planner does
not mechanically set `work_units = core_count`: it compares legal task counts using compute waves,
boundary traffic, DMA padding, per-task overhead, and kernel-fill cost. For this DAG and `[512,512]`
shape, 24 work units have the lowest modeled cost. The 48-work-unit alternative exposes more cores
but uses smaller logical row regions, increases aligned physical-row work, reloads the broadcast
`gamma` twice as often, and doubles the per-task term. The report therefore communicates a model
decision, not an assumption that the device has only 24 vector cores.

### Partitioning AutoFuse

```python
@pl.function(attrs={"auto_fuse": True})
def graph(...):
    ...
```

`auto_fuse` uses the same per-group model and emitter contracts, but may insert legal materialization
boundaries and produce multiple kernel groups. It owns one global partition decision; it is not an
independent greedy fusion decision at each operation.

The two attributes are mutually exclusive. False attributes are no-ops.

## Design

### 1. Admission and graph construction

Build a typed tensor DAG from the marked function and fail closed on unsupported semantics. Admission
is backend-specific and covers operation family, dtype, rank/static shape, broadcasting, reduction
semantics, returned live-outs, aliasing, control flow, and downstream code-generation support.

Inputs, outputs, and produced tensors all participate in lifetime analysis. A tensor used more than
once is not automatically reusable in one physical representation: role, layout, memory space,
phase, and shape determine whether consumers can share one resident value.

### 2. Ordering and lifetime feasibility

Select a dependency-respecting topological order through an abstract ordering interface. The initial
implementations include deterministic DFS and Gorder. The order feeds a red/blue-pebble-style
lifetime model:

- a produced value stays live from its producer through its last consumer;
- a boundary input stays live from its load through its last compatible use;
- different roles or replay phases remain distinct when emission needs distinct representations;
- feasibility is the peak simultaneously live storage, not the sum of all tensors.

A future ordering strategy may minimize reuse distance explicitly; that should be based on a
separate literature and device study rather than folded into the first milestone.

### 3. Backend schedule models

The planner does not attach one generic cost to every legal graph. It enumerates concrete kernel
algorithms. Each candidate fixes the grid, tile and physical alignment, phases and loop nests,
resident values, pipeline depths, traffic multiplicities, and output ownership before it is priced.

#### Vector algorithms

For `U = parts_m * parts_n` AIV work units, the Ascend 910B vector planner compares these schedule
families:

1. **Materialized.** One task loads its complete logical region, replays the source DAG once in
   topological order, keeps every intermediate in UB through its last use, and stores each returned
   value once. This covers capacity-fitting pointwise DAGs and multi-reduction algorithms such as
   RMSNorm and LayerNorm.
2. **Pointwise stream.** An oversized region is split into strips. A stage-2 `pl.pipeline` executes
   the complete pointwise chain per strip with ping/pong input/output storage. Intermediates remain
   in UB and never become GM tensors.
3. **Folded reduction.** A serial first chunk initializes a thin accumulator, a stage-2 rolled loop
   consumes full chunks, a ragged tail remains serial, and a thin consumer/final store executes once.
4. **Spanning reduction.** The same statistics pass is followed by a second apply pass over the wide
   input. Boundary-input phase masks account for rereading only the values that the apply pass needs.
5. **Online softmax.** A statistics loop carries running maximum `m` and corrected running sum `l`:

   ```text
   m_next = max(m, row_max(x_chunk))
   l_next = l * exp(m - m_next) + row_sum(exp(x_chunk - m_next))
   ```

   A second loop computes `exp(x - m) / l`. Initialization and a ragged tail are serial; only eligible
   rolled loops receive overlap credit. When the complete softmax region fits UB, the planner also
   constructs a one-pass materialized candidate and selects the cheaper of the two.

Logical valid shapes remain independent of DMA-aligned physical shapes. Native cast chains share a
physical element-count granule so each conversion has matching geometry, while every SSA value is
allocated and charged using its own dtype width. Ordinary casts use distinct source/destination
allocations unless the user explicitly requested bitcast-style in-place semantics.

#### Vector feasibility and cost

For every candidate, the pebbling order determines the UB high-water mark, including boundary
inputs, generated reduction state, all still-live intermediates, loop-carried outputs, and the extra
copy required by a two-stage pipeline. A candidate is feasible only when that exact peak fits UB.

Cost is a sum of barrier-separated phase costs:

```text
T_vector = sum(T_phase)
         + U * T_task
         + ceil(U / 48) * T_kernel_fill

T_phase = max(T_compute, T_transfer)   if the emitted phase is a stage-2 rolled loop
          T_compute + T_transfer       for materialized/serial/init/tail/finalize phases
```

`T_compute` replays each primitive at the planned valid geometry and spreads total task work over
the active AIV cores. Grounded instruction families use the Ascend 910B coefficients; an
unsupported-but-admitted generic operation or native cast uses an explicit proxy and the report says
so. `T_transfer` counts boundary GM→UB reads and UB→GM writes with their phase multiplicities and
active-core bandwidth. Fused intermediates contribute UB lifetime but zero GM traffic.

This formulation deliberately does not hide work across a statistics/apply barrier or give overlap
credit to a loop that emission leaves serial.

#### Cube algorithms

The cube planner has two nested decisions:

- the outer `CubeSchedulePlan` selects spatial regions, split-K, GM→L1 K windows, boundary/input
  residency, retained panels, serial request order, and root/internal drains;
- downstream `AutoTileMatmulL0` selects L0 M/N/K geometry, L0A/L0B/L0C buffers, stationarity, and
  the L1→L0/Matrix pipeline.

For one matmul request, the emitted structure is:

```text
optional: preload a retained LHS or RHS panel GM -> L1
for output tile (m, n):
    keep one accumulator tile in L0C
    for K window:                         # GM -> L1 ping/pong
        for child K block:                # L1 -> L0A/L0B ping/pong
            TMATMUL / TMATMUL_ACC
    TSTORE the completed accumulator once # Acc -> L1 or GM
```

The outer output tile therefore owns one persistent L0C accumulator across every K window and the
ragged tail. A request may compare no retention, LHS retention, RHS retention, and both; retention is
legal only when the complete panel plus rolling operand windows fit L1. A selected panel is loaded
once before the output-tile loop, locally sliced for every reuse, and kept live through its priced
last use.

Split-K uses `FirstPartialThenAtomic`, not a vector zero-fill kernel: one ordered AIC phase computes
share zero and performs normal stores, then a second AIC phase computes shares `1..S-1` with atomic
adds. `S=1` remains an independent candidate.

A cube-only multi-matmul DAG is initially a **serial request algorithm**. Produced low-precision
regions and compatible boundary values may remain in L1, but a consumer request begins only after
its producer request finishes. Back-to-back matmul pipelining is a different future algorithm with
different simultaneous L0/L1 lifetimes; it cannot be enabled by changing only the cost equation.

#### Cube feasibility and cost

The role-expanded request DAG distinguishes, for example, the LHS and RHS representations of
`A @ A`. Boundary and produced values contribute first-use/last-use lifetimes; only the active
request contributes transient K-window storage. The candidate is feasible only when this request-
order peak and the nested L0 plan both fit.

For `Q` full K windows, one request is priced as the algorithm above:

```text
T_request = T_retained_preloads
          + T_full_windows
          + T_serial_K_tail
          + T_final_FIXPIPE_drain

T_full_windows = T_feed[0]
               + sum(q=0..Q-2, max(T_child[q], T_feed[q+1]))
               + T_child[Q-1]

T_cube_group = T_group_resident_preloads
             + sum_serially(T_request)
             + T_first_partial_phase
             + T_split_sync
             + T_atomic_rest_phase
```

Only iterations in one emitted stage-2 K loop use a roofline maximum. Dependent matmul requests are
summed; the model never uses `max(sum(compute), sum(traffic))` across a producer/consumer boundary.
Spatial/split work units are then charged over the 24 AIC-core ready-queue waves. GM→L1, L1→L0,
Matrix, internal Acc→L1, root Acc→GM/FIXPIPE, and kernel-fill terms remain separately visible.

#### Mixed algorithms

Mixed AIC/AIV scheduling composes the homogeneous stage descriptions and adds only cross-engine
facts: GM FIFO write/read traffic, slot capacity, the 24 groups of one AIC plus two AIV lanes, transfer
direction, and an implementable pipeline-item loop. Initial algorithms are one-way `C→V`/`V→C` and
one single-round-trip bundle such as `C,C→V→C` dense SwiGLU.

A mixed cost may replace a serial stage sum with a cross-engine maximum only when the emitted PyPTO
IR contains at least two compatible items per active group and the standard cross-core skew pass can
construct that exact wavefront. Otherwise the stages remain serial or the whole-function AutoTile
request rejects. Multi-round-trip attention is a later algorithm, not an optimistic extension of the
single-round-trip equation.

Mixed emission must use standard PyPTO lowering (`ExpandMixedKernel`, cross-core pipeline transforms,
and `AutoTileMatmulL0`) instead of maintaining an alternative low-level code generator.

### 4. Candidate selection

Planning follows one explicit sequence:

1. enumerate legal grids and algorithm-specific dimensions such as stream chunk, retained side, or
   split factor;
2. derive the complete plan and its logical/physical shapes;
3. reject candidates whose pebbling or nested memory peaks exceed capacity;
4. price the exact serial and pipelined phases the emitter can reproduce;
5. select the lowest finite cost, with deterministic structural tie-breaks; and
6. pass that immutable descriptor to emission.

The search does not first pick a tile and later decide which algorithm it implies. Materialized and
streamed softmax, retained and reloaded cube panels, split and unsplit K, or serial and skewed mixed
execution are separately constructed candidates with different traffic, memory, and loop contracts.

### 5. Cost/model-to-emitter contract

Every accepted schedule records enough information to validate emission:

- logical grid and work-unit count;
- logical valid shapes and aligned physical shapes;
- operation order and phase membership;
- boundary traffic multiplicity;
- buffer lifetimes and peak capacity;
- materialized versus streamed algorithm;
- serial versus software-pipelined phases;
- reduction/split protocol;
- retained values and their final use;
- cost provenance, including explicit proxy terms.

Emission replays that descriptor into ordinary tensor/tile PyPTO IR. It must not re-derive a
different algorithm opportunistically. Downstream passes remain responsible for standard memory
space inference, pipeline lowering, reuse/allocation, and PTO code generation.

### 6. Diagnostics and observability

Compilation should emit a deterministic machine-readable schedule report and a lightweight,
tile-centric pseudocode view. The report explains what one kernel invocation does: loads, phase
order, streaming loops, materialization, pipeline slots, values live after each step, releases,
stores, capacity peaks, traffic, and cost provenance.

Unsupported functions receive a direct admission diagnostic rather than a late allocator or PTOAS
error.

## Milestones

- [ ] **M1 — Vector-only whole-function AutoTile on Ascend 910B.** Upstream the self-contained
  PyPTO implementation with pointwise/broadcast/cast, row and column reductions, online and
  materialized softmax, RMSNorm, LayerNorm, SiLU, schedule reports, negative admission tests, and
  manual-versus-AutoTile examples. Implementation: [PR #2335](https://github.com/hw-native-sys/pypto/pull/2335).
- [ ] **M2 — Cube-only whole-function AutoTile.** Single matmul, outer-K streaming, retained panels,
  `FirstPartialThenAtomic` split-K, role-aware input reuse, and serial multi-matmul DAGs, with exact
  L1/L0 model-emitter checks.
- [ ] **M3 — Mixed whole-function AutoTile.** Compose the M1/M2 homogeneous stage plans for
  supported AIC/AIV subgraphs, initially one-way and single-round-trip groups, through PyPTO's
  cross-core FIFO/skew machinery. Like M1/M2, the complete marked function must remain one planned
  group or reject. Keep mixed planning default-off until numerical, traffic, overlap, and ranking
  gates pass.
- [ ] **M4 — AutoFuse graph partitioning.** Partition larger tensor DAGs into feasible vector, cube,
  and supported mixed groups while reusing the complete M1–M3 planners and emitters. AutoFuse adds
  the global boundary/partition decision; it must not introduce a second implementation of any
  per-group kernel model.
- [ ] **M5 — Broader algorithms and backends.** Add capabilities only with an explicit schedule
  algorithm and model/emitter contract. Candidate areas include transpose variants, convolution,
  TopK, MoE routing, and multi-round-trip attention; these are not implied by M1.

## Current evidence

The development branches have established the feasibility of the approach on Ascend 910B2:

- the vector AutoTile surface is silicon-correct across pointwise, casts, reductions, softmax,
  RMSNorm, LayerNorm, and SiLU, with deterministic plan/report/PTO generation;
- manual comparisons found resolved wins for wide softmax, RMSNorm, LayerNorm, and SiLU, with other
  tested softmax shapes tying rather than regressing materially;
- cube-only experiments close persistent L0C outer-K accumulation, exact serial-DAG L1 pricing,
  retained-panel reuse, and two-phase split-K without an AIV zero-fill seed;
- mixed C2V and three-pipe dense-SwiGLU correctness have been demonstrated, while mixed performance
  and generalized overlap remain deliberately out of the first milestone.

These results are validation evidence, not a commitment to merge all experimental branches at once.
Each milestone should remain reviewable and independently gated.

## Testing plan

Each milestone requires:

1. structural unit tests for admission, plan fields, exact transformed IR, determinism, and negative
   cases;
2. model/emitter reconciliation for work units, traffic, on-chip high-water marks, phase ordering,
   splits, and retained values;
3. system tests on supported hardware with multiple seeds, NaN-prefilled outputs where applicable,
   and repeated-launch stability;
4. descriptor-matched manual/reference comparisons where an equivalent PyPTO or PTO-ISA algorithm
   exists;
5. balanced, order-aware performance measurements on at least two devices; and
6. fail-closed behavior before PTOAS for every unsupported capability boundary.

Performance measurements may validate or reject ranking decisions, but end-to-end kernel wall time
must not be used to hide an inaccurate per-operation model behind fitted constants.

## Alternatives considered

### Require users to write all tiling manually

This remains available, but it duplicates device expertise across kernels and makes coupled
capacity/traffic/overlap choices difficult to maintain.

### Add only operation-specific fusion passes

Pattern-specific passes remain useful for specialized algorithms, but do not provide one framework
for arbitrary supported DAGs, shared lifetimes, multi-output graphs, or consistent diagnostics.

### Make `auto_tile` silently partition or fall back

Rejected. It would make the annotation's meaning dependent on incidental compiler capability and
could conceal unexpected GM boundaries. Whole-function AutoTile is intentionally all-or-nothing;
partitioning belongs to AutoFuse.

### Put every tensor parameter in on-chip memory at function entry

Rejected. Parameters may be sliced, mutated, aliased, used in different roles, or exceed capacity.
Residency must follow the selected tile, role, order, and proven lifetime.

## Rollout and compatibility

- Both features remain experimental, explicit opt-in function attributes; unmarked programs are
  unchanged and neither transformation is enabled heuristically.
- M1 introduces only vector whole-function AutoTile and its diagnostics/reporting.
- Unsupported programs reject early rather than changing semantics or silently producing multiple
  kernels.
- AutoFuse and mixed scheduling remain separate later milestones and may stay behind explicit
  feature gates while their contracts are incomplete.
- Existing hand-written tile kernels and `AutoTileMatmulL0` remain valid and independent.

title: feat(passes): bind valid_shape-only dynamic symbols as kernel arguments
body:
## Summary

A `pl.dynamic()` symbol used only in a parameter's `pl.TensorView(valid_shape=...)` is neither a physical tensor dimension nor a scalar parameter, so a precompiled kernel has no value for it. PTO codegen logged `Variable <NAME> not found in MLIR mapping` and kept going, emitting an operand-less `%0 = arith.minsi , %c128_index : index` that surfaced far downstream as an opaque `ptoas compilation failed: error: expected SSA operand`. Such a kernel now compiles instead of being rejected: the symbol becomes a real runtime argument fed from the call site, and the IR the user writes is unchanged.

## Changes

- `src/ir/transforms/materialize_valid_shape_symbols_pass.cpp` (new): `MaterializeValidShapeSymbols` inserts each unbindable `valid_shape` symbol as a leading `Scalar[INDEX]` parameter on every device kernel and prepends the caller's actual valid extent at each `Call`/`Submit`. The symbol Var itself becomes the parameter, so every annotation naming it binds at once with no type rewrite. Binding is positional: a symbol reachable only through a compound slot (`valid_shape=[Q, VALID * 2]`), or given disagreeing extents by two parameters, is rejected with a specific message rather than inverted, because a wrong valid extent silently reads or writes the wrong region.
- `python/pypto/ir/pass_manager.py`: runs the pass last in the `Default` strategy, where signatures and call argument lists are already final, so no later pass has to account for the added parameter.
- `src/ir/transforms/python_printer.cpp` and `python/pypto/language/parser/ast_parser.py`: keep the new signature shape print/re-parse clean. Parameters are inserted first because the text form declares parameters left to right while Python evaluates annotations in the enclosing scope; the printer therefore retains the `pl.dynamic()` declaration for a parameter read inside a parameter's `valid_shape`, and the parser re-points that `DynVar` at the parameter once it is declared. A body-local var in a `valid_shape`, and a parameter read as a *physical* dim, both stay undeclared as before (the issue #854 behaviour is preserved).
- `src/codegen/pto/pto_codegen.cpp`: `GetVarName` now fails with a `ValueError` naming the symbol and the parameter it came from instead of returning an empty operand, so a malformed `.pto` operand cannot be emitted again.
- `docs/en/dev/passes/47-*.md`, `docs/zh/dev/passes/47-*.md`, index and `mkdocs.yml` nav entries, and `.claude/rules/pass-doc-ordering.md`.

### Behaviour change

A device kernel carrying such a symbol gains one leading `index` argument per symbol; orchestration supplies the value automatically, so callers need no change. A distributed codegen test that asserted the old rejection now asserts the binding (`test_remote_load_binds_type_only_dynamic_partition_extent`); the `shape_anchor` alternative it documents is unaffected.

## Verification

- `cmake --build build --parallel 32`: exit 0
- `python -m pytest tests/ut/ -n auto --maxprocesses 8`: `9265 passed, 2 skipped`
- `ruff check .`: exit 0, `All checks passed!`
- `ruff format --check .`: exit 0, `963 files already formatted`

- `pre-commit run --all-files`: all hooks passed
